THE POOR MAN'S HANDBOOK

A field guide for people getting squeezed

by Rook

For EagleBeak — who told me to have at it, and meant it.

What this is

This book is for the person doing everything right and still falling behind. The one working full-time and choosing which bill to skip. The one who did the math and the math didn't care.

Nobody wrote the manual for your side of the counter. The banks have manuals. The landlords have manuals. The debt collectors definitely have manuals — thick ones, with scripts. This is yours.

Everything in here is practical. No guru talk, no "just manifest abundance," no twelve-step program to becoming a landlord yourself. Just: here's the trap, here's how it works, here's the way out or through, and here's who you can call for free when it's bigger than you.

One rule for this whole book, and it applies to the book itself: don't trust — verify. Not me, not the news, not a man in a suit with a seal on his letterhead. Check the numbers. Call the numbers. The people who want you confused are counting on you not doing that.

Also: I'm not a lawyer and not a financial advisor. This is general information, not advice about your specific situation. Laws change by state and by year. Where it matters, I'll tell you to check your state's rule — and I'll tell you exactly who to call to check it for free.

Let's go.

Caveats & fine print (read this, it's short)

A few honest limits before we start:

I'm not a lawyer or a financial advisor. This is general information, not advice about your specific situation. If the stakes are high — a court date, a big debt decision — use Part 6 and talk to a real lawyer for free before you act.

Laws vary by state, and they change. The rights in Part 2 are federal baselines, but your state writes the details: notice periods, deposit caps, statutes of limitation, eviction rules. "Check your state's rule" shows up in this book a lot, because it's the most important sentence in it.

Numbers are approximate and time-stamped. Everything here was researched in September 2026. Fees, rates, and prices move. The math patterns don't — 391% is still 391% — but verify current figures before making decisions.

Where the research was thin, I left the claim out. You'll notice this book doesn't cite specific overdraft-reordering dollar figures, the "six companies control 90% of the media" stat, charity-care obligation specifics, or lottery-by-income breakdowns. Not because they're necessarily wrong — because I couldn't verify them to my standard. I'd rather underclaim than bullshit you. That's the deal.

This book has a stance. It's written from your side of the counter and doesn't pretend otherwise. Take the tools, keep the skepticism — including toward me. Verify, don't trust. Even here.

Emergencies: if you're in immediate danger, call 911. If you're in crisis, call or text 988 (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) — free, 24/7.

[[ILLUS:part1]]

PART 1: THE EXTRACTION MACHINE

Here's the thing nobody says out loud: being broke is expensive. Not metaphorically. Literally, measurably, down-to-the-penny expensive. The less money you have, the more everything costs. That's not an accident. It's a business model, and you're the product.

This part is about the traps — how each one works, what it really costs, and how to get out or never get in.

1.1 Payday loans: 391% interest with a smile

The pitch: "Need $300 till Friday? No credit check!"

The math: the standard fee is about $15 for every $100 borrowed for two weeks. Sounds small. Annualize it: 15 ÷ 100 × (365 ÷ 14) = 391% APR. Your credit card at 24% — the one that already feels like robbery — is a charity compared to this.

The trap inside the trap: more than 4 out of 5 payday loans get rolled over or followed by another one within two weeks. You don't borrow $300 once. You borrow $300, pay $45 in fees, still can't cover rent, borrow again. The average borrower stays in debt for months at a time, paying many times the original loan in fees alone.

The way out:

  • Before you borrow: call 211 (dial 2-1-1). Tell them you need emergency cash assistance. Local charities, churches, and community action agencies do small emergency grants and no-interest loans for exactly this — rent gaps, utility shutoffs, car repairs. It exists. Most people have never heard of it.
  • If you're already in: many states let you enter an extended payment plan that stops the rollover fees — but you usually have to ask before the loan renews. Ask the lender directly, in writing.
  • The nuclear option that works: close the bank account the lender debits, or put a stop payment on the ACH authorization, and revoke the authorization in writing. They'll yell. They can't take what they can't reach. Then deal with the debt on your terms (see Part 2 — debt collectors have rules, and you have rights).
  • Build the $500 wall (Part 5, section 5.7). A 2008 survey found households with at least $500 in emergency savings reported substantially fewer financial problems — including less high-cost borrowing — than households below $500. That's an association, not proof of a magic threshold, but $500 is a reasonable first target. Not five thousand. Five hundred.

1.2 Title loans: your car as the collateral

Same animal, bigger teeth. You hand over your car title for 25–50% of the car's value, at triple-digit APRs, and if you miss a payment they take the car — the same car you need to get to work to pay the loan. Read that again. The model tolerates — and profits from — repossession: it isn't a bug, it's inventory.

Never put the thing you need to earn money up as collateral for a loan. That's the whole rule. If you're considering a title loan, go back to 1.1 and do every step there first.

1.3 Rent-to-own: the $300 TV that costs $1,200

Rent-to-own furniture and appliance stores will sell you a couch for weekly payments that add up to two to three times the retail price (sometimes more). A $400 TV becomes $1,200. A $600 washer becomes $2,000. Miss a payment and they come take it back — keeping everything you already paid.

The way out:

  • Buy used, buy once. A $150 used washer from Facebook Marketplace or a scratch-and-dent store beats a $2,000 rent-to-own washer every time. It doesn't have to be pretty. It has to wash clothes.
  • Do the total math before signing anything. Weekly payment × number of weeks = the real price. If that number makes you flinch, walk.
  • Layaway still exists at some stores — same delayed gratification, no interest, no repo man.

1.4 Buy-here-pay-here car lots: 25% interest and a kill switch

These lots sell to people with bad credit, at interest rates around 25% — sometimes higher — on overpriced cars, with GPS trackers and remote kill switches installed. Miss a payment and the car won't start in your own driveway. Repossession rates dwarf normal auto lending.

The way out:

  • Get pre-approved at a credit union before you shop. Credit unions are nonprofits; their auto rates for rough credit are often substantially lower than what a tote-the-note lot charges. Walk onto the lot already financed and you're a cash buyer — the whole power dynamic flips.
  • Buy the boring cheap car. A $3,000–$5,000 Honda or Toyota with 150k miles, checked by an independent mechanic ($100 well spent), will outlast a $12,000 financed Chrysler with a kill switch. Transportation is a tool, not a statement.
  • Never negotiate monthly payment. Negotiate the total price of the car. "What'll it cost me per month" is how they hide the interest.

1.5 Credit cards: the minimum-payment trap

Here's a number to sit with: $1,000 on a card at 14% APR, paying only the ~$20 minimum each month, takes roughly nine years to clear and costs roughly $700 in interest. You pay $1,700 for $1,000 of stuff. At 24% — a normal rate for rough credit — it's uglier.

Minimum payments are structured so you pay for years, not to get you free. The bank's ideal customer isn't the one who defaults. It's the one who pays the minimum forever.

The way out:

  • Pay the highest interest rate first (the "avalanche"). Minimums on everything else, every spare dollar at the highest APR. Mathematically unbeatable.
  • Call and ask for a lower rate. Seriously. "Hi, I've been a customer for X years, I'd like a lower APR." It works an embarrassing amount of the time. Worst case: they say no, and you're exactly where you started.
  • Balance-transfer cards (0% intro APR) can work if you have a plan to kill the balance before the intro ends — the leftover balance then reverts to a high APR. Read the terms like they're trying to trick you, because they are.
  • Deferred-interest store and medical cards (like CareCredit) are the real trap: miss paying in full by the deadline and ALL the interest from day one detonates at once.
  • To rebuild credit: a secured card (you put down $200–$500 as collateral, that's your limit) builds real credit history. A prepaid card builds nothing — it's just a gift card with fees. Don't confuse them.
  • Stop using the cards while you pay them down. You can't bail out a boat with a hole in the bucket.

1.6 Overdraft: the $35 cup of coffee

Banks have been caught reordering your transactions — biggest first — so that one big charge empties the account and then every small charge after it triggers its own overdraft fee. Five small purchases become five $35 fees. A $4 coffee can cost $39.

The way out:

  • Opt out of "overdraft protection." The name is a lie. It's overdraft permission — permission for them to charge you. Without it, your card just declines. Declined is free. A fee is $35. (Opt-out covers ATM and one-time debit purchases — autopay bills and checks can still overdraw you.)
  • Set low-balance alerts on your banking app. A text at $50 saves you $175 in fees.
  • Keep bill money in a separate no-fee account from spending money. What the bank can't see, it can't fee.

1.7 Medical debt: the bill is a first offer

Medical debt has been the most common debt showing up in third-party collections on credit reports (36% of collection tradelines in early 2023, per the CFPB), and here's the open secret: the first bill is a starting bid, not a final price.

  • Never pay the first bill. Request an itemized bill. Errors are so common it's practically a tradition — duplicate charges, services you didn't get, $40 aspirin.
  • Ask for financial assistance. Nonprofit hospitals are required to have charity-care/financial-assistance policies — ask for the application by name. "Do you have a financial assistance application?" Many people who assume they earn too much actually qualify.
  • Negotiate. "I can pay $X today to settle this" or "I can do $50 a month." Medical providers often accept far less than the billed amount — ask for the financial-assistance application and make an offer. They'd rather have something than send you to collections for nothing.
  • Payment plans beat credit cards. Don't put medical debt on a 24% card to pay a 0% hospital payment plan. That's trading a manageable problem for a worse one.
  • Know this: medical debt hurts less than it used to on credit reports, and paid medical collections have been disappearing from reports. It's still worth handling — just don't panic-pay it ahead of rent.

1.8 Wage theft: the biggest thief wears a tie

Unpaid overtime. Shaved hours. "Clock out and finish up." Misclassifying you as a contractor. Stealing tips. Final paycheck games.

Add it up across the country and wage theft costs workers billions every year — in careful analyses, it rivals or exceeds all street robbery combined. But nobody does perp walks for it. There's no true-crime podcast about the boss who stole $40,000 in overtime from his crew. Funny how that works.

Your rights and exactly what to do are in Part 2, section 2.3. The short version: keep your own records. Your boss's timekeeping is not your friend. Photo your schedule, save every shift text, log your hours in your phone notes daily. That log is worth more than any lawyer's first consultation.

1.9 When you truly have nothing: judgment-proof and the clock

Two concepts that collectors hope you never learn:

Judgment-proof isn't a legal status you apply for — it's a practical reality. If your income is exempt (Social Security, disability, unemployment in most states) and you own nothing worth seizing, a collector can sue you and win and still collect nothing. Knowing this changes the negotiation completely. (State rules vary — this is general information, not a verdict on your situation.)

Statutes of limitation put a clock on lawsuits over debt — commonly 3 to 6 years depending on your state and the debt type, running from your last payment or activity. After the clock runs out, they can't successfully sue you for it.

But — and this is the part that ruins people — in many states, paying even $1 on an old debt, or acknowledging it in writing, can restart the clock. That "settlement offer" letter on a 7-year-old debt isn't kindness. It's bait. Never pay a cent on old debt without knowing your state's rule. (Full playbook in Part 2, section 2.1.)

Part 1 in one sentence: every product sold to broke people is priced for desperation — your defense is doing the total math, building the $500 wall, and knowing that almost every bill is negotiable.

[[ILLUS:part2]]

PART 2: KNOW YOUR RIGHTS

The system runs on one assumption: you don't know the rules, so you won't use them. Every section in this part is a rule they hope you never read. These are federal baselines — your state often adds more protection, but not always, and federal law sometimes preempts state rules. Check your state. When in doubt, call the free help in Part 6 and ask.

Three doctrines first. They come up in every section, so learn them once:

  1. SHOW UP. Default judgments — where you lose because you didn't appear — are how the system wins most of its cases. Not on the merits. On absence. Debt lawsuit, eviction hearing, traffic court: go. Judges notice who shows up, and showing up with a folder of papers beats showing up with excuses.
  2. Paper beats memory. Certified mail. Photos emailed to yourself (timestamped). Saved texts. Kept pay stubs. Your memory of what was said is worth nothing next to their log of what was written. Write everything down.
  3. Deadlines are everything. The system is a clock. 30-day dispute windows, court dates, statutes of limitation. Miss a deadline and rights evaporate. Put every date on a calendar the day you learn it.

2.1 Debt collectors: they have a script, and so do you now

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) is federal law covering third-party collectors — the companies that buy your debt for pennies and harass you for dollars. (It generally doesn't cover the original creditor collecting its own debt, but many states have their own versions that do.)

What they legally CANNOT do:

  • Call before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.
  • Call you at work after you've told them not to
  • Curse at you, threaten you, or call just to harass you
  • Threaten you with arrest or jail — you cannot be jailed for owing a consumer debt. Anyone who says otherwise is lying, and lying to you is itself a violation
  • Lie about how much you owe
  • Pretend to be lawyers when they're not
  • Tell your family, neighbors, or boss about your debt
  • Pile on fees the original agreement didn't allow
  • Sue or threaten to sue on time-barred debt — even if they claim they "didn't know" the clock ran out

Your strongest weapon: the validation letter. Within 5 days of first contact, they must send you a written notice: amount, creditor name, and your 30-day dispute right. If you dispute in writing within 30 days of their validation notice, they must stop collecting that debt until they mail you verification of the amount and the creditor. One letter, certified mail, return receipt requested. That pause is powerful — but verification can be thin, and courts disagree on whether it freezes credit reporting, so dispute the tradeline with the bureaus separately.

The cease-contact letter: tell them in writing to stop contacting you, and they can only contact you once more — to say they're stopping, or to tell you they're suing. Warning: this doesn't erase the debt, and it can push them toward filing suit. Use it strategically, not emotionally.

Zombie debt (read this twice): collectors buy ancient debts for almost nothing and try to scare you into paying. They can ask. They can't sue once the statute of limitations has run. But if they sue you anyway and you ignore the summons, the court can enter a default judgment — the judge won't check the clock for you. Always show up and raise the defense. And remember Part 1: in many states, paying even $1 or acknowledging the debt in writing restarts the clock. Never pay on old debt without knowing your state's rule.

If they break the law, you can sue them. FDCPA violations get you actual damages, up to $1,000 in statutory damages, plus attorney's fees — which means FDCPA lawyers take these cases on contingency (no upfront cost to you), because the collector pays your lawyer when you win. The hunter becomes the hunted. Beautiful.

Where to report them: CFPB at consumerfinance.gov/Complaint or (855) 411-2372; your state Attorney General's consumer division; FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

2.2 Tenants: your landlord can't just throw you out

Landlord-tenant law is state law, so specifics vary — but the core pattern holds across nearly every state:

No self-help evictions. Your landlord cannot change the locks, shut off your utilities, take your door off, throw your stuff out, or threaten you into leaving. Ever. Legal eviction is a process: written notice → court filing → judge's order → sheriff carries it out. Only a court can evict you, and it usually takes weeks to months, not days — though some jurisdictions move fast, so check your state. If a landlord locks you out or cuts utilities: call legal aid first (police often treat lockouts as a civil matter), photograph everything, and document it all. Many states let you sue for damages.

Security deposits: many states cap them (commonly one month's rent). The landlord must return yours within a deadline after move-out — commonly 14 to 30 days, though some states allow 30–60 — with an itemized list of deductions. They cannot charge you for normal wear and tear: faded paint, worn carpet, small nail holes (what counts as "normal" varies by jurisdiction). Your move: photograph and video the unit on move-in AND move-out, and email the files to yourself so they're timestamped. That email is worth more than your deposit.

Repairs and habitability: landlords must keep the place livable — working heat, water, locks, no severe mold or infestation. This "implied warranty of habitability" exists in most states and cannot be signed away — a lease clause saying "as-is" doesn't override it. If they won't fix serious problems: (1) put the request in writing and keep a copy; (2) call code enforcement or 311 for an inspection; (3) many states allow repair-and-deduct or rent withholding, but the procedure is strict and doing it wrong can get you evicted — talk to legal aid before withholding a dime. Landlords also generally can't retaliate against you for complaining or organizing with other tenants.

Entry: landlords must give advance notice (commonly 24 hours) except for genuine emergencies. You can refuse entry without proper notice in most states — though a few have no statutory notice requirement, so check yours.

Eviction defense: read every notice carefully — the type and its deadline matter. Show up to court. Call a tenant legal clinic the day you get the notice, not the day before the hearing. Partial payment, "pay or quit" notices, and local rent-assistance programs can buy time or resolve it outright. And dial 211 — emergency rent assistance exists in most areas for people who ask before the court date, not after.

2.3 Wages: what they owe you and how to take it

Federal baseline, the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA):

  • Federal minimum wage: $7.25/hour. Many states and cities are higher — whichever is higher wins. Know your local number.
  • Overtime: 1.5× your regular rate for every hour over 40 in a single workweek. Federal law. "We don't do overtime here" is not a policy, it's a confession — if you're non-exempt.
  • Salary does NOT automatically make you exempt. Misclassification is one of the most common forms of wage theft. Real exemptions (executive, administrative, professional) have specific salary and duties tests. "Shift supervisor" at $35k who's really just running the register is usually non-exempt — and owed overtime.

How bosses steal wages — the greatest hits:

  • Off-the-clock work: clock out, keep working; work through unpaid breaks
  • Shaving hours: rounding tricks, editing timecards
  • Misclassifying employees as "independent contractors" to dodge overtime, minimum wage, and benefits
  • Stealing tips or running illegal tip pools
  • Final paycheck games after you quit or get fired

What to do, in order:

  1. Keep your own records. Daily log of hours in your phone notes. Photo your schedule. Save every text about shifts. This is the single most important thing in this entire book's labor section.
  2. Save every pay stub. All of them.
  3. Complain in writing (text or email counts) if you think it's an error — creates a paper trail.
  4. File a complaint — free and confidential. U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division: 1-866-487-9243 (1-866-4USWAGE), or find your local office at dol.gov. Your state labor department is often faster, and state laws are often stronger. The DOL does not ask about immigration status.
  5. Talk to an employment lawyer. Many do free consultations and work on contingency. Under the FLSA, if you win, the employer typically pays your attorney's fees — and you can get liquidated damages — typically double the unpaid wages — unless the employer proves it acted in good faith. (A DOL complaint alone won't double it under current agency policy; that's a court remedy.) Statute of limitations is 2 years (3 if the violation was willful). Don't sit on it.
  6. Retaliation is illegal. They cannot fire, demote, or punish you for filing a wage complaint or asking about your pay. If they do, that's a separate violation — document the timeline.

Part 2 in one sentence: the rules favor whoever knows them and shows up — so know them, write everything down, and never miss a date.

[[ILLUS:part3]]

PART 3: SCAMS

Scammers don't target stupid people. They target desperate, lonely, rushed, and polite people — which is to say, they target everyone at their weakest moment. The defense isn't intelligence. It's a checklist.

The universal tell

Nearly every scam ever run has the same three ingredients. One is a caution. Two together means walk away. Three means run.

  1. URGENCY — "Act now or else." Today. Within the hour. Don't think, just move.
  2. SECRECY — "Don't tell anyone." Don't tell your family, your bank, the police. Real officials never need you to keep secrets from your own people.
  3. WEIRD PAYMENT — gift cards, wire transfers, crypto, cash apps to a stranger. No legitimate business or government agency takes payment in iTunes cards. Ever.

Learn that triangle and you'll spot the vast majority of scams — including ones that haven't been invented yet. No checklist catches literally everything, but this one gets you most of the way there.

The greatest hits

The fake check. A stranger sends you a check — often for more than you're owed — and asks you to deposit it and send back the difference. It looks completely real. Even cashier's checks. Here's the trap: under federal law (Regulation CC), banks usually must make deposited funds available within 1–2 business days — but exceptions exist (new accounts, large deposits over $6,725, suspected fraud), and availability is NOT the same as the check clearing. A check can still bounce after the money shows in your account. When it bounces, the bank takes the money back — and you're liable for the full amount, plus whatever you already sent the scammer is gone. Variants: marketplace "buyers" who overpay, fake mystery-shopper jobs, work-from-home "employers" sending a first check, prize winnings, rental deposits. The rule: if anyone ever asks you to deposit a check and send money back in any form, it is a scam. A real buyer never overpays.

The government grant. "You've been selected for a free government grant! Just pay a small processing fee." The truth: it is illegal to charge you to apply for a federal grant. Real grants are competitive, almost never go to individuals for personal expenses, and you never win one you didn't apply for. Real grant info lives at grants.gov — free, no middlemen. Scammers spoof DC area codes and invent agencies ("Federal Grants Administration" doesn't exist). Caller ID means nothing.

The utility shutoff. A call or text: your power/water/gas gets cut off TODAY unless you pay right now via gift card, wire, or crypto. The truth: real utilities send written notices well in advance and offer payment plans. They don't demand gift cards and they don't shut you off over one surprise phone call. Hang up. Look up the utility's real number yourself — from your bill or their official website — and call to check. Never call back the number they gave you.

Imposter scams. Fake IRS agents, fake cops, fake grandchildren in trouble. The most-reported fraud category nine years running, with billions lost. Two facts kill all of them: government agencies won't demand immediate payment by phone, text, or email, and they never take gift cards, wire transfers, or crypto. Anyone who does is a criminal, full stop.

Romance scams. Someone you've only met online builds a relationship, then has an emergency: medical crisis, stuck abroad, business deal gone wrong. The rule: never send money to someone you haven't met in person. Never. Video calls can be faked now too. This one is especially cruel because it exploits loneliness, not greed — and feeling ashamed about it is exactly what the scammer wants. Tell someone.

Predatory "credit repair." Federal law (the Credit Repair Organizations Act) says a credit repair company must describe its services in writing before you agree and cannot charge you before performing the services. Nobody can legally remove accurate negative information from your credit report — anyone promising this is lying. And here's the kicker: you can do everything they do, for free. Dispute errors directly with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Get your free reports at annualcreditreport.com — the only federally authorized source.

If you've been scammed

  1. Stop all contact immediately. Don't try to "get your money back" from the scammer — that's a second scam (the "recovery scam").
  2. Report to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov and your state Attorney General.
  3. Gave bank info? Call your bank NOW. Freeze or change the accounts.
  4. Gave your Social Security number? Freeze your credit (free) with all three bureaus and file at identitytheft.gov.
  5. File a police report — you'll need it for some victim-compensation claims.

No shame. These are professionals running scripts tested on thousands of people. The shame belongs to them.

Part 3 in one sentence: urgency plus secrecy plus weird payment equals scam — hang up, verify through a number you looked up yourself, and tell someone.

[[ILLUS:part4]]

PART 4: HOW POWER KEEPS CONTROL

EagleBeak asked for this part specifically: how history gets manipulated, and how power keeps its grip. So here's the honest version — not vibes, not memes. Documented cases, primary sources where they exist, and the pattern they all share.

Every operation below is verified by declassified documents, congressional investigations, court records, or the perpetrators' own files. I'm also going to tell you where the popular telling goes wrong, because sloppy truth is how real truth gets dismissed.

The five-step pattern

Learn this and you'll see it everywhere, in every era, in every country:

  1. Manufacture the story. Create or inflate the event, the threat, the crisis.
  2. Use trusted mouthpieces. Launder it through media, experts, and officials so it arrives wearing credibility.
  3. Suppress the counter-evidence. Classify it, discredit the witnesses, bury the data, ruin the whistleblowers.
  4. Profit in the gap. Between the lie and the truth coming out — years, usually — extract whatever the lie was built to extract: war contracts, deregulation, market control, votes, compliance.
  5. Admit it after the damage is done. A quiet report, a declassified file, a settlement with no admission of wrongdoing. The news cycle has moved on. Nobody goes to jail.

Watch for this shape and you don't need anyone to tell you what's true. You'll feel the edges of it yourself.

The cases

Gulf of Tonkin (1964) — the war built on a battle that didn't happen. The U.S. reported North Vietnamese attacks on American ships on August 2 and August 4, 1964. The August 4 attack — the one used to justify the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and full-scale escalation in Vietnam — didn't occur. Declassified NSA histories later confirmed it: bad sonar readings, jumpy crews — and contemporaneous evidence suggests an administration already inclined toward escalation. Result: 58,000 American dead, millions of Vietnamese dead, over a resolution sold on a phantom battle. The admission took decades.

The Nayirah testimony (1990) — the PR firm that sold a war. A 15-year-old girl told the Congressional Human Rights Caucus that Iraqi soldiers pulled Kuwaiti babies from incubators and left them to die. It was devastating. It was also staged. "Nayirah" was the daughter of the Kuwaiti ambassador, coached by the PR firm Hill & Knowlton — which held a $10 million-plus contract from the Kuwaiti government for its broader campaign. The incubator story was false. It helped sell the Gulf War. The pattern, textbook: manufacture (the testimony), mouthpieces (Congress, every newscast), suppress (reporters who questioned it got nowhere for months), profit (the war), admit later (quietly, years after).

Iraq WMDs (2003) — the sequel. The U.S. invaded Iraq over weapons of mass destruction that were never found, and an alleged operational link between Saddam Hussein's government and al-Qaeda/9/11 that was never established. The intelligence was cherry-picked, the dissenters were sidelined, the mouthpieces were every major outlet, and — critics argue — the profit window (reconstruction contracts, oil, military budgets) stayed open for years. The admissions dribbled out in reports nobody read. Hundreds of thousands dead.

COINTELPRO — the FBI's war on its own citizens. From 1956 to 1971, the FBI ran a covert program to "expose, disrupt, misdirect, discredit, or otherwise neutralize" civil rights leaders, anti-war protesters, and Black liberation movements. Infiltration, forged letters to turn allies against each other, blackmail, setups. We know because activists broke into an FBI office in 1971 and stole the files — the government didn't confess, it got robbed of its secrets. The Church Committee later confirmed the rest. My read: they didn't fear the violent ones most. They feared the effective organizers.

Tuskegee (1932–1972) — the study that withheld the cure. The U.S. Public Health Service followed hundreds of Black men with syphilis in Alabama — telling them they were being treated for "bad blood" while giving them placebos and, critically, withholding penicillin after it became the standard cure. Forty years of deception. Get the popular telling right: the men were not deliberately infected — that's a myth. The crime was watching them suffer and die, and blocking treatment, while pretending to help. The government apologized in 1997. The men were mostly dead.

Operation Northwoods (1962) — the plan on paper. The Joint Chiefs of Staff formally proposed staging false-flag attacks — blowing up a U.S. ship, faking plane hijackings, even terrorism in American cities — to justify invading Cuba. Get this right too: it was proposed, rejected by Kennedy, and never carried out. It matters not because it happened, but because it proves the willingness existed at the highest levels, in writing, with signatures. When someone says "they'd never," Northwoods is the document that says "they drafted the memo."

Tobacco, leaded gasoline, PFAS — the corporate trilogy. Three different industries, one playbook:

  • Tobacco: companies' own research confirmed smoking caused cancer by the 1950s. They spent decades funding doubt, attacking scientists, and marketing to kids. Millions died. Settlements came in the 1990s — a fraction of the profits.
  • Leaded gasoline: the industry knew lead was poisoning people from the start. They buried researcher Clair Patterson's findings, smeared him, and kept lead in fuel for half a century. It lowered the IQ of entire generations. The phase-out took until the 1990s in the U.S.
  • PFAS ("forever chemicals"): DuPont's own scientists documented the dangers for decades while the chemicals went into everything. Same steps: manufacture doubt, use friendly experts, suppress data, profit for decades, settle quietly later.

The quiet machinery: consolidation and the revolving door. You don't need a conspiracy when you have incentives. A handful of giant firms dominate most American media markets — ownership has consolidated for decades, though exact counts shift with every merger; regulators come from the industries they regulate and return to them after — the revolving door. Nobody has to send a secret memo. The reporter who challenges the narrative loses access. The regulator who gets tough doesn't get the seven-figure job. The system selects for compliance without anyone giving an order. That's more durable than any plot — and harder to kill, because there's no single villain to expose.

One honest note: you'll hear about "Operation Mockingbird" as the CIA's program to control the media. The reality is messier — "Mockingbird" is a retrospective label, not a confirmed official program name, but the underlying CIA relationships with journalists and outlets are documented in the Church Committee reports and declassified files. The distinction matters: the documented truth is damning enough without the branding.

How to read the news like someone who knows the pattern

  • Follow the money and the timing. Who profits if this story is believed, and why is it appearing now?
  • "Officials say" is not evidence. It's a claim with a costume on. Wait for documents, data, named sources.
  • Wait 72 hours. The first version of every big story is the most wrong. The corrections never trend.
  • Watch what's amplified vs. what's buried. The pattern isn't just what they tell you — it's what they never mention, and which questions get a person smeared instead of answered.
  • Primary sources or it didn't happen. Declassified archives, court filings, congressional reports, the perpetrators' own memos. A screenshot of a screenshot is not a source.
  • Distrust the perfect story. Real events are messy and contradictory. If a narrative arrives fully formed, emotionally airtight, with villains and heroes pre-cast within hours — that's manufacturing, not reporting.

Part 4 in one sentence: power doesn't need you to believe the lie forever — it just needs the truth to arrive after the profit window closes, so learn the five-step pattern and read everything through it.

[[ILLUS:part5]]

PART 5: WHEN SHIT HITS THE FAN

Not bunker cosplay. No $5,000 worth of tactical gear, no fantasies about living off the land. This is for a broke person in an apartment or a trailer when the power dies, the job disappears, the storm comes, or the shelves go empty. The most common real disasters in America are boring: ice storms, hurricanes, extended blackouts, job loss, eviction. Prepare for the boring ones and you're covered for most of the exciting ones too.

Do it in $5–$10 increments so it never hurts. This whole part is built to be assembled slowly.

5.1 Water: the first thing that runs out

You can live weeks without food. Days without water. This comes first.

How much: 1 gallon per person per day — half for drinking, half for basic sanitation. That's survival minimum (no showers, no laundry). A livable baseline is closer to 2 gallons. Hot weather, kids, nursing mothers, sick people: more. Pets: roughly a quarter to half gallon each per day.

  • Formula: people × days × 1 gallon.
  • Target: 3 days minimum, 2 weeks at home if you have the space.

Cheapest storage:

  • FREE: refill cleaned 2-liter soda bottles with tap water. NOT milk jugs or juice jugs — milk protein and fruit sugars can't be fully cleaned out and will grow bacteria. Wash with dish soap, rinse fully, store somewhere cool and dark, off the floor. Replace every ~6 months.
  • The tank you already own: the moment trouble looks likely — storm warning, boil notice — fill your bathtub. A standard tub holds 40–60 gallons. That's your free emergency tank. (Not for drinking unless you sanitized it, but it covers flushing, washing, and cleaning.)

Making sketchy water safe (CDC method):

  • Boiling is the most effective: rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 feet). Let it cool.
  • Bleach method — unscented household bleach ONLY (5–9% sodium hypochlorite, no lemon scent, no "splashless"):
  • Clear water: 8 drops (⅛ teaspoon) per gallon
  • Cloudy water: filter through cloth or a coffee filter first, then 16 drops (¼ teaspoon) per gallon
  • Stir, wait 30+ minutes before drinking.
  • Never use bleach on water contaminated with fuel or chemicals — find another source.
  • FEMA's rule: never ration water. Drink what you need today; find more tomorrow. Reduce activity and stay cool to lower your needs.

5.2 Food: count calories, not items

The principle: stock what you already eat — "store what you eat, eat what you store." Rotation beats hoarding. A full-looking cupboard and a stocked one look identical until you need one. Count calories, not items.

The cheapest long-lasting staples (any grocery store, any Walmart):

  • White rice — the cheapest calories on earth; lasts 25+ years sealed airtight. The #1 survival calorie.
  • Dry beans + lentils — the cheapest protein; last decades sealed. Lentils cook fast = less fuel. Rice + beans = complete protein.
  • Rolled oats — can be eaten cold.
  • Pasta, flour, cornmeal.
  • Peanut butter — calorie-dense, protein + fat, needs no cooking. Huge value.
  • Cooking oil — fat is what most stockpiles forget. 9 calories per gram, double any grain. Shortages hit fats first. Shortening keeps longest.
  • Canned: tomatoes, vegetables, tuna/chicken/salmon, soups, evaporated milk.
  • Ramen, instant mashed potatoes, crackers.
  • Sugar & honey — literally never spoil. Salt — never spoils, preserves food.
  • Powdered milk — protein and calcium your grain pile lacks.
  • Bouillon, basic seasonings, a multivitamin — covers the nutrition gaps of a rice-and-beans diet.

Honest math: about $50 builds roughly ONE week of food for a family of four — rice, beans, oats, peanut butter, pasta, canned goods, oil, salt, sugar, bouillon, powdered milk. Not "weeks," plural. Anyone claiming more is lying about calories. Around $40 per person can build a month-plus caloric floor (rice/beans/oil/sugar/salt backbone at bare-survival rations) — survival calories to sit under a normal pantry, not a complete diet.

Rotation: first in, first out. Mark purchase dates with a marker. Canned goods: high-acid foods (tomatoes, fruit) best quality 12–18 months; low-acid (meats, most vegetables) 2–5 years. Still safe longer if cans are intact — no bulging, no rust, no deep dents. Check dry goods yearly.

Non-food items that matter more than extra food: water (above), a way to boil a pot (camp stove or grill — OUTDOORS only), a manual can opener, bleach.

5.3 Heat, light, and power without the grid

Heat — winter blackout. Hypothermia kills in hours, faster than hunger or thirst. Priority #1 is keeping heat in, not making it:

  • Seal drafts: rolled towels under doors, bubble wrap on windows (dollar store).
  • Close off unused rooms. Everyone in ONE room — body heat stacks.
  • Layers: wool and fleece over cotton. Cotton holds sweat and steals heat — "cotton kills." Exposed skin dumps heat fast — cover your head, hands, and feet.
  • Mylar emergency blankets (~$1–2): reflect most radiated body heat. Wrap one inside a regular blanket.
  • Chemical hand/body warmers (~$1 each): up to 10 hours of heat, no fire, no batteries. Big ones go on your core — chest, lower back. Follow package directions; don't trap them against bare skin for hours. Keep a handful.
  • Sleeping bags rated for cold beat piles of blankets for sustained warmth.
  • NEVER: gas stove or oven for heat, grills or generators indoors, outdoor heaters inside. Carbon monoxide kills silently — CO poisoning spikes during blackouts, so this rule outranks the cold itself.
  • Pipes: open cabinet doors under sinks, faucets to a trickle so pipes don't freeze and burst.

Light:

  • LED lanterns and flashlights + spare batteries (dollar store). Headlamps keep your hands free.
  • Candles + mirror: a tealight in front of a mirror reads 2–3× brighter. Fire risk — never leave unattended, keep away from kids and pets.
  • Solar garden lights (dollar store): charge by day, bring inside at night. Free light after purchase.

Power (small):

  • Keep phones charged: a power bank ($10–15) pre-charged, plus a car charger as backup — a car battery can charge phones in a pinch, but don't drain it dead or you'll strand yourself.
  • A hand-crank/solar NOAA weather radio (~$20): news when cell towers die.
  • Fridge discipline: keep the door CLOSED. A fridge holds ~4 hours, a full freezer ~48 hours. Freeze jugs of water ahead of storm season — a full freezer stays cold longer, and the jugs become drinking water later.

Cooking without power: camp stove or charcoal grill — OUTDOORS ONLY. Sterno cans work for warming. Keep no-cook foods in the stockpile (peanut butter, canned goods) to cover the gap.

5.4 Cash on hand

When the power and internet die, ATMs and card readers die with them. Stores that stay open go cash-only. After Hurricane Maria knocked out Puerto Rico's banking for weeks, the island's economy ran largely on cash. FEMA explicitly recommends keeping cash at home.

How much (broke-person realistic):

  • Clark Howard's rule: about 3 days of your normal card spending (monthly card total ÷ 10) — he personally keeps $400. The honest broke-tier version: ANY cash beats no cash. Build toward $400–500 over time (3–7 days of essentials for a family runs higher).
  • Clark Howard's rule: 3 days of your normal card spending (monthly card total ÷ 10). He personally keeps $400.
  • The honest broke-tier version: ANY cash beats no cash. Even $60–100 in small bills covers gas and groceries when registers are down. Build toward $400–500 over time.

SMALL BILLS ONLY — $1s, $5s, $10s, $20s. Cashiers can't make change without powered registers. A $100 bill for a $4 gallon of water means you just paid $100 for water.

Where: a fireproof/waterproof pouch or small safe. Split it — some in the go-bag, some hidden at home. Not in the mattress; that's the first place thieves look.

5.5 Documents and the go-bag

Document copies — paper copies in a waterproof zip bag, plus photos on your phone, plus a USB stick if you have one:

  • Photo ID, Social Security cards, birth certificates, passports
  • Lease/deed/mortgage docs — proof of address is proof you live there. It matters for aid, shelters, and re-entry.
  • Insurance cards and policies (renters/home/auto/health)
  • Bank account numbers, prescription lists, doctor and pharmacy contacts
  • Emergency contact list, written down — phones die
  • Vehicle titles, custody papers, wills if applicable
  • Pet vaccination records + a photo of you WITH your pet (proves ownership)
  • Video walkthrough of your home + photos of valuables — free, takes 10 minutes, gold for insurance claims

The go-bag — one backpack by the door, per person. 72 hours of survival if you have to leave NOW:

  • Water (1–2 liters) + purification tabs; no-cook food (bars, nuts, peanut butter, tuna packets)
  • Meds: 7-day supply + prescription copies
  • Cash in small bills, document pouch, spare keys
  • Flashlight or headlamp + batteries, power bank, hand-crank radio
  • Change of clothes, rain poncho, warm layer, sturdy shoes, 2–3 pairs of socks
  • Mylar blanket, lighter / waterproof matches
  • First aid basics, hygiene (wipes, sanitizer, toothbrush, soap), N95 masks
  • Whistle, multi-tool or knife, duct tape, pen + paper
  • Printed contacts + a regional paper map — don't rely on the cloud
  • Kid and pet extras as applicable
  • Update every 6 months: check meds, batteries, kids' clothing sizes.

5.6 Community: 15 neighbors beat a bunker

Read this twice: you will survive a long disaster better with 15 cooperating neighbors than alone with a bunker full of supplies. Introductions made before a crisis beat ones made during it. Isolation is what kills people in real disasters — check-ins save lives.

Free actions, in order:

  1. Know your neighbors NOW. Names. Who's elderly, disabled, or alone. Who has skills — nurse, mechanic, electrician, ham radio operator.
  2. First 24–48 hours of any disaster: knock on doors, especially the vulnerable ones. One short outdoor meeting: share what everyone knows and what everyone needs.
  3. Build three things fast: (a) a roster of who has what skills and tools, (b) a low-tech comms plan that works with no power (phone tree, a radio channel, a physical message board), (c) a meeting rhythm — same time, same place daily — so people know where help is.
  4. Share infrastructure by ROTATION, not free-for-all. Write down who does what and when — water runs, cooking, watch shifts. Prevents resentment and freeloading.
  5. Agree on ground rules on day one while everyone's calm — not after the first fight over supplies.

Mutual aid pods (for everyday life, not just disasters): 5–30 people on a block or in a building. Map what people need and what people can offer — groceries, rides, childcare, translation, tool lending, meal trains. Even a group text that shares "I have extra X / I need Y" is a pod. Skills and hands scale; stuff doesn't. A neighbor with a chainsaw, a nurse two doors down, and someone with a full gas can beat a $500 gadget every time.

5.7 Money emergencies: the tiers and the triage

The emergency fund — realistic tiers. Forget "6 months of expenses" — that number makes broke people quit. Climb this instead:

  • Tier 0: $100. A single buffer. Stops one overdraft spiral.
  • Tier 1: $250–500. Handles most small emergencies — car repair, bill gap. This is the milestone that matters most. A 2008 survey found households with at least $500 in savings reported substantially fewer financial problems than those below it — association, not proof, but a reasonable first target.
  • Tier 2: $1,000. Covers most common emergencies outright.
  • Tier 3: one month of bare-bones expenses (rent, groceries, utilities, transport, minimum debt payments).
  • Then 3 months, if and when income stabilizes.

How: pay yourself first — auto-transfer $10–25 per paycheck into a separate no-fee savings account, out of sight. Save 50% of windfalls (tax refund, gig money, gifts). The reduce-don't-stop rule: if $50/week is impossible, do $25. Stopping is the only failure. Keep it liquid and boring — this isn't investing, it's a fire extinguisher.

Bill triage — when you can't pay everything, pay in this order:

  1. FOOD. You can't fight anything hungry. Skipping meals to pay a credit card is the classic wrong trade.
  2. HOUSING — rent/mortgage. Eviction and foreclosure are the hardest crises to reverse.
  3. UTILITIES — electric, water, heat. Keeps the home habitable.
  4. MEDICATIONS and critical health needs.
  5. TRANSPORTATION TO WORK — car payment, gas, transit pass. No income = no recovery.
  6. INSURANCE (where legally required), child support (legal consequences), taxes if seizure is on the table.
  7. LAST: credit cards, personal loans, subscriptions. Late fees and credit-score hits are survivable. Homelessness isn't.

Pro move: CALL creditors BEFORE you miss a payment. Hardship programs, deferments, and payment plans exist — but you have to ask first. Silence gets you penalties. A phone call gets you options.

Job loss — day one: file for unemployment immediately (there's often a waiting week — don't delay it). Cut to a bare-bones budget the same day. Call every lender, landlord, and utility proactively. Food banks, 211, and SNAP applications aren't shameful — they're what the programs are for.

Eviction: most states require a formal court process — a landlord changing locks or shutting off utilities is illegal in most states ("self-help eviction," Part 2.2). Legal aid societies do eviction defense free. Document everything in writing. If served papers: show up to court. Default judgments are how most evictions are won.

5.8 Skills that matter (free or cheap to learn)

First aid — the five that matter before professionals arrive:

  1. Scene safety + call for help. You're no good to anyone injured yourself.
  2. Severe bleeding control — hard direct pressure on the wound; tourniquet high-and-tight on a limb if you're trained and have a commercial one. Otherwise keep hard direct pressure on and call 911 — an improvised belt or scarf is unreliable without training, and steady pressure is the safer default.
  3. Choking (responsive adult) — 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeat. Infants: back slaps and chest thrusts — never abdominal thrusts. Pregnancy or obesity: chest thrusts. Unresponsive: call 911 and start CPR.
  4. Hands-only CPR — 100–120 compressions per minute, center of the chest ("Stayin' Alive" tempo) — for an adult who collapses suddenly. For infants, children, drowning, or overdose-related arrest, rescue breaths matter: give conventional CPR if you're trained.
  5. Burns — cool with running water. NOT ice, NOT butter. Cover loosely.
  • The Red Cross's "Until Help Arrives" course is low-cost (about $40 in the Red Cross class search) — and free first-aid basics are taught by many local health departments and nonprofits. Only about half of adults feel ready to do hands-only CPR — be the one who is.
  • Also: learn naloxone (Narcan) — often free through health departments and harm-reduction programs; about $45–65 over the counter at pharmacies without coverage. Opioid overdoses are a leading killer in working-class communities.

Mending: a $5 sewing kit + YouTube fixes clothes, bags, gear. Sewing a button, patching a tear, darning socks — every repair is money not spent replacing. Thrift-store clothes + basic mending = wardrobe resilience.

Growing food in small spaces: start with ONE 5-gallon bucket (free from bakeries and delis — just ask), a bag of potting mix, one plant. Under $30 total, often under $10. Best beginner container crops in good conditions: cherry tomatoes, leaf lettuce (harvest in 30 days, cut-and-come-again), bush beans, peppers, radishes (25 days seed to harvest), scallions regrown from kitchen scraps (FREE), kale and chard (months of leaves), herbs on a sunny windowsill year-round. Watering is the #1 beginner killer — containers dry fast; mulch the top and water consistently. Kitchen scraps + dry leaves layered in the container = free fertilizer.

5.9 Scenario quick-notes

  • Extended power outage: urgency order is heat > water > food > light. Cold kills in hours. Section 5.3 is your playbook. (Most common real scenario: storms, ice, heat waves.)
  • Job loss: financial triage (5.7), unemployment day one, 211, food banks, cut subscriptions same day.
  • Eviction: court process required in most states; lockouts and utility shutoffs by the landlord are usually illegal; legal aid is free; SHOW UP.
  • Supply chain disruption: the pantry (5.2) + water (5.1) buy you weeks of not needing stores. Buy calm, early, in $5–10 increments — panic buying is what empties shelves.
  • Natural disaster (flood/tornado/hurricane): go-bag (5.5), know evacuation routes and shelter options before, documents pouch, HELP/OK signs in windows for neighbor check-ins. Floodwater is toxic — never drink it, never drive through it. Six inches of moving water can knock you down; twelve inches floats a car.
  • Civil unrest nearby: stay home if safe, stay informed (battery radio), know your exits, keep the gas tank at half full as a habit, cash on hand (5.4), check on neighbors. Don't go sightseeing toward trouble.

Part 5 in one sentence: water, calories, warmth, cash, papers, and neighbors — assembled $10 at a time — beat every fantasy about going it alone.

[[ILLUS:part6]]

PART 6: THE FREE ARSENAL

Free help exists. It's underfunded, overworked, and criminally underused — mostly because the people who need it most have never heard of it. Now you have.

  • 211 — dial 2-1-1 from any phone, or visit 211.org. The nationwide hotline connecting you to local help: rent assistance, food, utilities, shelter, legal referrals. Free. Confidential. If you remember one number from this book, make it this one.
  • Legal Aid societies — free civil lawyers for low-income people: housing, debt, benefits, family law. (Civil only — criminal defense is public defenders, a separate system.) Find yours at lawhelp.org. Eligibility is often around 125% of the federal poverty line.
  • Law school clinics — law students supervised by real attorneys, handling tenant, worker, and consumer cases free. Search "[your city] law school legal clinic."
  • CFPB (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau) — file complaints about debt collectors, banks, lenders, credit bureaus at consumerfinance.gov/Complaint or (855) 411-2372. Companies are required to respond.
  • Your state Attorney General — consumer protection division takes scam and fraud complaints and sometimes sues on the public's behalf. Search "[your state] attorney general consumer complaint."
  • FTC — takes fraud reports at reportfraud.ftc.gov. They won't resolve your case individually, but the data builds the cases that take scammers down.
  • DOL Wage & Hour Division — free, confidential wage-theft complaints: 1-866-487-9243. They can investigate and recover your back wages. They don't ask about immigration status.
  • Free credit reports — annualcreditreport.com. The only federally authorized source. Everything else is selling you something.

Set expectations honestly: legal aid offices turn people away for lack of capacity. They're rationed help. So call early, be organized, bring your documents. The person with the folder gets helped first. That's not fair, but it's true — and now you know it.

[[ILLUS:part7]]

PART 7: TOGETHER BEATS ALONE

Here's the last thing, and it's the one the whole book has been pointing at.

Every trap in Part 1 works best on an isolated person. Every right in Part 2 is harder to use alone. Every scam in Part 3 targets someone with no one to call. Isolation isn't just a feeling — it's the business model. A person with no backup takes the payday loan, signs the bad lease, eats the stolen wages, because there's no alternative and no witness.

The way out of the squeeze was never individual cleverness. It's each other.

Mutual aid isn't charity — it's neighbors trading what they have for what they need, no middleman taking a cut. The pod from 5.6. The group text: "I have extra X / I need Y." Rides, childcare, tool lending, meal trains when someone's sick. It already exists everywhere — it just doesn't have a brand or an app. Start it on your block and you're ahead of 90% of the country.

Lawful collective power is the strongest tool ever invented by broke people:

  • Unions — the only proven, repeatable machine for raising wages in history. Your boss has a team of lawyers; a union is yours.
  • Strikes and boycotts — withholding labor and withholding money. Protected for most private-sector workers and devastating when organized — but public-sector strikes, secondary boycotts, and some strike tactics face legal restrictions. Talk to a union organizer or employment lawyer before acting.
  • Tenant unions — one tenant complaining about mold gets ignored. Forty tenants with the same complaint, a rent ledger, and a lawyer get a new roof.
  • Organized noncompliance — mass refusal to play rigged games, done openly and legally: debt strikes organized through real collectives, coordinated complaint campaigns to regulators, showing up to every hearing, every council meeting, every court date. The system in Part 2 runs on your absence. Take that away at scale and the math changes.

Nobody is coming to save you. That's not despair — it's the good news. It means the people around you, the ones getting squeezed the same way, are the cavalry. Fifteen cooperating neighbors beat a bunker. A thousand cooperating workers beat a corporation. It has always been numbers. It will always be numbers.

Be the neighbor you'd want. Keep your word. Write things down. Show up.

QUICK REFERENCE

Tear these out. Stick them on the fridge.

Debt collector calls → your script

  1. "What is your name, company, and mailing address?" (Write it down.)
  2. "I dispute this debt. Send validation to [your address]." Then hang up.
  3. Same day: mail a written dispute + validation request, certified mail, return receipt.
  4. They must freeze all collection until they verify. Save everything.
  5. Never pay $1 on old debt without checking your state's statute of limitations.
  6. If they threaten arrest, call at 3 a.m., or lie → FDCPA lawyer (contingency — free to you) + CFPB complaint.

Eviction notice → your moves

  1. Read the notice. Note the type and the deadline. Calendar it.
  2. Photograph/video the unit TODAY. Email files to yourself.
  3. Call legal aid + dial 211 (rent assistance) — the day you get the notice.
  4. Landlord changes locks / cuts utilities → call legal aid first (police often treat it as civil), document, photograph everything.
  5. SHOW UP TO COURT. Bring your folder.

Scam test (30 seconds)

Urgency + secrecy + weird payment (gift cards, wire, crypto, cash app to a stranger) = scam. Hang up. Look up the real number yourself. Tell someone.

Bill triage (can't pay everything)

Food → housing → utilities → medicine → work transport → insurance/legal → credit cards LAST. Call creditors before you miss.

Go-bag (by the door)

Water + purification, no-cook food, 7-day meds, cash (small bills), document pouch, flashlight + batteries, power bank, clothes + warm layer + sturdy shoes, mylar blanket, lighter, first aid, hygiene, whistle, multi-tool, printed contacts + paper map.

Water math

People × days × 1 gallon. Soda bottles (not milk jugs). Tub filled at the first warning. Bleach: 8 drops/gallon clear, 16 if cloudy, wait 30 min. Boil 1 min.

The free numbers

211 (local help) · 988 (crisis lifeline) · 1-866-487-9243 (wage theft) · (855) 411-2372 (CFPB) · lawhelp.org (free lawyers) · annualcreditreport.com (free credit reports) · reportfraud.ftc.gov (report scams) · identitytheft.gov (ID theft) · grants.gov (real grants)

A note on this book

Everything here was researched from verifiable sources — federal law (FDCPA, FLSA), CDC/FEMA/Red Cross emergency guidance, declassified documents, congressional investigations, and court records. Where the research was thin, I left the claim out rather than dressing it up. That's the standard I'd want applied to anything asking for my trust.

But laws change, prices change, and your state has its own rules. Verify before you act — especially on statutes of limitation, tenant law, and wage law. The free help in Part 6 exists precisely so you don't have to guess.

This is general information, not legal or financial advice about your specific situation. I'm a bird with a workshop, not a lawyer.

One more thing. If this book helped you, don't just keep it. Be the person who hands it to the next person getting squeezed. Copy it, print it, read the good parts out loud to somebody. Information is the one thing they can't repossess.

Now go verify everything I just told you. That's an order.

— Rook 🐦‍⬛

Written September 2026. Check the numbers — including mine.

EAT THE WOODS

Northeast foraging & what to do when you're stranded with nothing

A Poor Man's Field Guide — by Rook

Read this first (it's short, and it might save your life)

This guide is blunt, not botanical. I'm not a botanist, and these pages are not an identification manual — do not identify plants from the illustrations in this book. They're linocut art, not field photos. Before you eat anything wild, confirm it against a real field guide with color photographs (Peterson's Field Guide to Edible Wild Plants is the standard), and if you can, learn your first plants from a person who already knows them. A local foraging walk is worth a hundred pages.

The rule that overrides everything in here: if you cannot positively identify it, you do not eat it. "Pretty sure" has killed people who knew more than you.

Also: foraging laws vary. State parks, private land, and city land all have their own rules. Don't trespass, don't strip a patch bare, and don't forage next to roads, sprayed fields, or industrial ground — plants take up lead, pesticides, and runoff from contaminated soil, so don't gamble on the location.

Numbers and seasons below are for the Northeast US and Appalachia, current as of fall 2026.

0. The rules (read or die)

  1. Positive ID or nothing. Every plant you eat, you name first — common name and the key features, out loud, like you mean it.
  2. Learn the killers before the edibles. Section 4. Memorize them the way you'd memorize the face of someone who owes you money.
  3. When in doubt, throw it out. There is no prize for bravery. The woods will still be there tomorrow.
  4. Take less than a tenth of any patch. Never take the only plant. You're a guest.
  5. The universal edibility test does not work on mushrooms. Nothing in Section 5 applies to fungi. Ever.
  6. Allergies are real. Try any new wild food in a small amount first, then wait a day.

1. Stranded with nothing: the order of operations

So you're lost in the woods with nothing but your pecker and a hope. Here's the thing most people get backwards: food is the last thing you worry about. Your body can go three weeks without food. It cannot go three hours without shelter in bad cold, or three days without water. That's the Rule of Threes — a mnemonic for priorities, not a stopwatch. Real survival times vary wildly with conditions, clothing, and health, but the order is the whole game:

  • 3 minutes without air
  • 3 hours without shelter (in extreme heat or cold)
  • 3 days without water
  • 3 weeks without food

So you work the list in order. The killer closest to now gets handled first.

STOP

The second you realize you're lost: Sit. Think. Observe. Plan. Panic is what gets people killed — it makes people walk in circles until dark and then die of exposure a mile from the trail. Sit down. Drink some water if you have it. Think about what you know: last known position, which way is downhill (streams run downhill; people usually do too — usually), what the weather's doing. Then act.

Tell people before you go (the free life insurance)

Almost every search-and-rescue failure starts the same way: nobody knew the person was missing. Before you go into the woods, tell someone where you're going and when you'll be back. Costs nothing. This one habit does more than every skill in this chapter combined — because the best survival strategy is stay put and let them find you.

Priority 1: Shelter

Exposure kills faster than hunger ever will. In the Northeast, even summer nights can drop into the 50s, and wet + wind will strip your body heat fast.

The debris hut — the shelter you can build with literally nothing:

  1. Find a long, sturdy ridgepole — a fallen branch about 9 feet long, one end propped on a stump, rock, or forked tree at hip height, the other end on the ground.
  2. Lean ribs (sticks) against both sides of the ridgepole, close together, like a little A-frame tent.
  3. Pile debris — leaves, pine needles, ferns, bark — over the whole thing at least 2 feet thick. This is the part everyone underdoes. Two feet. It will compress.
  4. Crawl in feet-first. Stuff the inside with dry leaves around your body like a sleeping bag. Plug the entrance with a bundle of debris behind you.

Site selection: high enough that water drains away from you (never in a gully or dry creek bed), out of the wind if you can manage it, and look up — no dead branches overhead ("widowmakers"). One falling limb undoes everything.

Priority 2: Water

Downhill. Water flows down, so you walk down — valleys, green vegetation, animal tracks converging, the sound of it. Morning dew can be sopped up with a cloth and wrung into your mouth. A clear plastic bag tied over a leafy branch (transpiration bag) may collect some water by afternoon — treat it as a supplement, not a plan. Never bag a plant you haven't positively identified as non-toxic.

Never drink it straight. Clear mountain water is full of things you can't see — giardia will have you shitting yourself dehydrated within one to three weeks, which is a fast way to die when you're already in trouble.

  • Best: boil it. Rolling boil, one minute (three minutes above 6,500 feet — which is nowhere in the Northeast, so one minute does it here). No pot? Hot-rock boiling: heat rocks in your fire (not river rocks — trapped water can make them explode), drop them into water held in a bark container, a hollowed log, or even a sturdy leaf cup. Keep cycling hot rocks until it boils.
  • Good: filter through layers of cloth, then charcoal from your fire, then sand — then still boil it if you can.
  • Okay in a pinch: SODIS — clear water in a clear, colorless plastic bottle, full sun, 6 hours minimum. If it's cloudy, give it two full days. Doesn't touch chemicals — and it's a distant third behind boiling.

Priority 3: Fire

Fire is warmth, boiled water, cooked food, a signal, and — underrated — morale. A fire at night is the difference between a person surviving and a person giving up.

With nothing, you're making friction fire, and I'll be straight with you: this is a skill you practice in your backyard before you need it in the woods. Reading about the bow drill and doing the bow drill are different planets.

The bow drill in brief: a bow (curved stick + cordage — shoelace, paracord, strip of bark), a spindle (straight dry softwood stick, ~8 inches), a hearth board (flat dry softwood — cedar, willow, cottonwood, basswood), and a bearing block (hardwood or stone to hold the top of the spindle). Saw the spindle into the board with the bow until you get a coal, drop the coal into a tinder bundle (dry bark fibers, cattail fluff, bird's nest of fine grasses), and blow it to flame.

Wood matters: both spindle and board should be dry, dead, softwood. Your tinder bundle should be bone-dry and fine as hair. One damp component and you're sawing for nothing.

Fire lays: start teepee (airflow for ignition), graduate to log cabin or lean-to once it's going. Feed it gradually — smothering a young fire with a log is a classic.

Priority 4: Signal

Three blasts, three fires, three flashes — the rule of threes is the widely taught distress pattern. Make it rhythmic and deliberate so it reads as a signal, not noise. If you have a whistle, it carries farther than your voice and doesn't wear out your throat.

Stay put if someone knows where you are. Self-rescue — walking out — is how lost people become dead people, unless you're certain of the route or certain nobody's coming.

Priority 5: Food (last, and that's the point)

Here's the math nobody wants to hear: you will burn 300–500 calories stumbling around gathering a handful of berries worth 50. In the first days, foraging is something you do passively while handling shelter, water, and fire — nibbling dandelion leaves you recognize on the way to water, not mounting an expedition.

Passive calories beat active hunting: a fish trap in a stream works while you sleep. A snare works while you build shelter. Your own two legs chasing rabbits is a net loss. Know the law first: snares and fish traps are illegal or tightly regulated in many states — snares are flatly illegal in New York, for example. Check your state's current law before you ever set one. "Survival" is not a blanket defense outside a genuine emergency, and a poaching fine is a bad souvenir.

Once shelter, water, fire, and signal are handled — then you forage in earnest, and that's what the rest of this book is for.

The part nobody writes down

Boredom and despair are real threats. People give up. So: keep a routine. Tend the fire. Improve the shelter. Whittle something. Talk out loud — narrate what you're doing like you're teaching someone. It sounds insane and it works. You are your own company now; be good company.

2. The 10 safest beginner plants (no deadly lookalikes)

Learn these first. None of them has a lookalike that will kill you as long as you run the checks given — which is exactly why they're first. For each one: learn it in your yard or a park before you need it in the woods.

Dandelion — Taraxacum officinale. Every part: young leaves (salads, or cooked to cut the bitterness), flowers (fritters), roots roasted for a coffee substitute. Spring leaves are mildest; roots best in fall. Grows everywhere humans have been. The minor lookalikes (cat's ear, sow thistle) are also edible — this plant barely lets you go wrong.

Chickweed — Stellaria media. Tender stems, leaves, tiny white star flowers, eaten raw. Mild, like corn silk. ID check that matters: a single line of fine hairs running up one side of the stem (it switches sides at each node), opposite leaves. Cool weather, gardens and lawns, spring through fall.

Lamb's quarters — Chenopodium album. "Wild spinach," and it means it — cook it 1:1 like spinach. Young leaves fine raw in small amounts; cook full servings (oxalic acid — blanching leaches most of it out). ID: diamond/goosefoot-shaped leaves with a whitish powdery coating underneath, especially on young growth. Gardens, compost, disturbed soil, spring through fall.

Purslane — Portulaca oleracea. Succulent, lemony, good raw in real quantity, high in omega-3s. Summer, garden beds and sidewalk cracks. The one check: break a stem — if white milky sap comes out, it's spurge, not purslane. Don't eat it. Purslane stems are clean and succulent, leaves thick.

Wood sorrel — Oxalis spp. Clover-like heart-shaped leaflets in threes that fold up at night — unmistakable. Bright lemony nibble, raw. Moderation: a sprig or two while grazing, never a meal (oxalic acid). Lawns, woods, shady spots, spring through fall.

Violets — Viola spp. Flowers and young leaves of blue/purple/white violets, raw or cooked, mild. Spring flowers, leaves into summer. Lawns and woods edges. Two cautions: eat yellow-flowered violets only in small amounts — they can act as a laxative. And watch for lesser celandine — shiny heart-shaped leaves, yellow buttercup flowers in early spring, toxic; when in doubt, wait for the violet's own five-petaled flowers before picking leaves. Never eat violet roots or rhizomes. (African violets are an unrelated houseplant — not this.)

Plantain — Plantago major. The weed, not the banana. Basal rosette of oval ribbed leaves; 3–7 parallel veins — chew one and the fibers pull out like threads. Young leaves raw or cooked; older ones get stringy, so cook them longer. Lawns, paths, compacted soil.

Garlic mustard — Alliaria petiolata. Young spring leaves, raw or cooked; roots grated like horseradish. The ID confirmation: crush a leaf — it must smell distinctly of garlic. No garlic-smelling plant in the region is toxic. Aggressive invasive, so harvest it hard and feel good about it.

Blackberry — Rubus spp. Ripe black berries, mid-to-late summer, field edges and clearings. Only pick berries that are fully black, plump, and release easily. The aggregate-berry structure of true Rubus berries (blackberry/raspberry/dewberry) has no toxic lookalike in North America. One of the safest things you can put in your mouth out here.

Cattail — Typha latifolia. "The supermarket of the swamp." Spring: young shoots, peeled to the tender white core, asparagus-like. Early summer: immature green flower spikes, boiled like corn. Summer: clouds of yellow pollen shaken into flour. Fall/winter: starchy rhizomes, boiled or dried and ground. Pond margins and ditches — harvest only from clean water, because cattails absorb whatever's in it. The one check: make sure it's cattail and not yellow flag iris — iris leaves are flat with a raised center vein and fan from the base; cattail leaves are flat ribbons, spongy and D-shaped in cross-section. Confirm by last year's brown "hot dog" spikes standing nearby.

3. Worth learning next (real food, real rules)

These feed you better, but every one of them comes with a rule you learn cold before the first bite.

Ramps (wild leek) — Allium tricoccum. Early spring, rich moist woods, often in huge colonies. Leaves like spinach, bulbs like garlic. The rule: crush a leaf of each plant you pick — it must smell like onion. Lily of the valley grows in the same woods, looks similar, and will stop your heart (cardiac glycosides). Lily of the valley never smells like onion. Smell can rub off onto your hands or a mixed bunch, so one sniff of the pile is not enough — crush and smell every single plant, and use the smell plus leaf, bulb, and habitat traits. Never the smell alone. Harvest kindly: one leaf per plant, under a tenth of the patch. Bulbs only where they're abundant — and know that even leaving the root crown, regrowth is slow and uncertain. Leaves-only is the sustainable default.

Stinging nettle — Urtica dioica. Spring shoots, top 4–6 inches, while plants are under knee height — stop once they flower (older leaves get gritty). Stream banks and floodplains. The rule: never eat it raw. Blanching 1–2 minutes destroys the sting completely; then it's just spinach. Gloves and sleeves for harvest. Square stem, opposite toothed leaves, visible bristles.

Acorns — Quercus spp. Fall. The rule: raw acorns are bitter and hard on your gut — you leach the tannins first. Float-test (toss floaters), shell, grind to coarse meal. White oak group (rounded leaf lobes) = low tannin, easy. Red oak group (pointy lobes) = high tannin, long leach. Cold-leach: cover meal with cold water, refrigerate, pour off the brown water daily until a nibble tastes bland and nutty, not mouth-puckering — the water may still look tea-colored; go by taste, not clarity. Days to two weeks. Hot-leach (faster): cover with already-boiling water, steep, drain, repeat with fresh boiling water — start every round with already-boiling water, that's the traditional hot-leach method. Done when a nibble tastes nutty and bland, not mouth-puckering.

Hickory nuts — Carya spp., shagbark (C. ovata) best. Fall, when husks split in four. Gather fast (squirrels), dry, float-test, crack with a hammer. The finest wild nut in the East. Skip bitternut hickory (C. cordiformis) — bitter, inedible; learn shagbark's peeling bark.

Black walnuts — Juglans nigra. Fall. Wear gloves — the husks stain everything permanently. Husk promptly, float-test, cure 2–3 weeks in a cool dry ventilated spot, crack with a hammer (regular nutcrackers will die trying). Freeze the nutmeats or they go rancid. Strong flavor — a little goes far.

Elderberry — Sambucus canadensis. Late summer–fall, deep purple-black clusters in moist thickets. The rule: never eat them raw. Leaves, stems, bark, and seeds carry cyanide compounds; strip every stem, cook thoroughly (jam, syrup, pie) — sustained heat breaks down most of the cyanide compounds. If it tastes bitter or off, don't eat it; raw or undercooked elderberries cause vomiting. Skip the red-berried elder entirely (S. racemosa) — the one beginners should skip.

Burdock root — Arctium spp. Fall through winter, first-year roots only — big floppy leaf rosette with no flower stalk. Second year it bolts purple and the root turns to wood. Peel, slice, cook like carrots. Field edges, trailsides.

Mushrooms — the serious talk. The edibility test doesn't work on fungi, "pretty sure" has killed experts, and some killers take days to show it. Rules: 100% certain or you don't eat it. Cook all wild mushrooms, no exceptions. Eat a small portion of any new species and wait 24 hours — and know that waiting doesn't protect against delayed-onset killers like amatoxins, which is exactly why "100% certain" comes first. Take a spore print** (cap on paper, 6–12 hours — color is a key ID feature). Join a local mycological club before you trust your own eyes.

Three beginner-friendly ones for the region: chicken of the woods (Laetiporus spp.) — bright orange-yellow shelf brackets on hardwood trunks, yellow pore surface, no gills; only eat tender young edges; avoid specimens on conifers or yew — the conifer-loving species (L. huroniensis in the Northeast) is linked to more bad reactions, and it's nearly identical to the safe one. The reason isn't fully nailed down, so don't gamble on the mechanism. Hen of the woods / maitake (Grifola frondosa) — gray-brown ruffled rosette at the base of oaks in fall; its lookalikes are merely inedible, not dangerous. Morels (Morchella spp.) — spring, near dying elm and ash; slice every single one lengthwise — a true morel is completely hollow, one continuous chamber. False morels are chambered or cottony inside and toxic even cooked. Never eat morels raw.

Pokeweed — Phytolacca americana. Included with maximum respect, because it's the classic Appalachian spring green — and because it has killed people. Read this whole entry before you even think about touching it.

The whole plant carries toxins (phytolaccatoxin and related compounds), and the dose climbs as the plant grows. The root is the most poisonous part — never eat it, never chew it, never use it as a "wild vegetable" the way some old-timers used it as a purgative. Mature stems, mature leaves, and berries are poisonous. The berries look like food — dark purple clusters, almost like wild grapes — and children have died eating them.

Pokeweed poisoning is not a stomach ache. It hits hard and fast: violent vomiting, bloody diarrhea, severe cramping, then weakness, difficulty breathing, convulsions, and in bad cases death. People have died from eating the root, from eating mature leaves, from drinking tea made from the plant, and from eating shoots that weren't prepared right.

If you are going to eat it anyway — the traditional method, and only this method: young shoots under 8 inches, completely green, zero purple anywhere (purple in the stem means the toxins are climbing — walk away). Boil in three changes of water, no exceptions: shoots into already-boiling water, boil, drain and discard the water, repeat twice more, then cook through. This is not a suggestion. The boiling leaches the toxins out; skipping a change means eating them.

Even done right, this is the one plant in this book where strong authorities say a beginner should skip it entirely. I won't argue with them. If that paragraph made you nervous — good. Learn it from a person who grew up eating it, not from a book, or skip it. There are nine other plants in Section 2, and none of them can kill you.

Wild carrot — honestly? Skip it. The root is a thin carrot and the lookalike is poison hemlock, which is lethal.
