Chapter 6 — How They Hit Back

Chapter 5 was the wins. This is the price tag.

Every movement in this book's history got hit back — infiltrated, surveilled, forged, framed, beaten, jailed, and in some cases killed. This isn't here to scare you off. It's here so you go in with your eyes open, because the people who built those wins didn't get to be surprised, and neither do you.

None of this is romantic. Arrest is not a badge of honor; it's a cost. Martyrdom is not a strategy; it's a failure mode. The movements that lasted were the ones that understood the other side's playbook cold — and planned for it.

COINTELPRO: The Playbook, Documented

From 1956 to 1971, the FBI ran a program called COINTELPRO — Counterintelligence Program. It started against the Communist Party USA. In the 1960s it expanded to the Ku Klux Klan, the Socialist Workers Party, the New Left (including SDS and SNCC), Black liberation groups (including the Black Panther Party, added as targets in September 1968), Puerto Rican independence groups, the American Indian Movement, and others.

It was secret until March 8, 1971, when a group calling itself the Citizens' Commission to Investigate the FBI burglarized an FBI field office in Media, Pennsylvania, and mailed the stolen files to journalists and members of Congress. Director Hoover formally ended the centralized program within the year. Then, in 1975–76, the U.S. Senate's Church Committee — formally the Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities, chaired by Senator Frank Church of Idaho — investigated the FBI, CIA, NSA, and IRS, and put the whole record on the table.

The record is ugly. A 1967 memo from Hoover to 22 field offices stated the purpose of the expanded program against Black activists: to "expose, disrupt, misdirect, discredit, or otherwise neutralize" Black leaders and organizations. The Church Committee's verdict: the Bureau "went beyond the collection of intelligence to secret action designed to 'disrupt' and 'neutralize'" its targets, using techniques "adopted wholesale from wartime counterintelligence" and "carrying a serious risk of physical, emotional, or economic damage" — in short, "a sophisticated vigilante operation aimed squarely at preventing the exercise of First Amendment rights of speech and association."

The documented tactics, from the Committee's record and the Bureau's own files:

  • Infiltration by undercover agents and paid informants, placed deep inside organizations.
  • Anonymous letters and forged correspondence — fake letters between members, fabricated documents, planted false information.
  • "Bad-jacketing" — falsely labeling genuine members as informants, which the FBI knew could get people harmed or killed by their own comrades.
  • Warrantless wiretapping and "black bag" break-ins — illegal entries to plant bugs or steal documents.
  • Pressure on the outside — contacting employers, landlords, donors, and journalists with derogatory material to get targets fired, evicted, defunded, or smeared.
  • Provocation — pushing embedded members toward more extreme or violent action, so the group could be discredited or criminalized.

Read that list twice. It's not ancient history — it's a menu. Every one of those tactics has a modern equivalent, and the digital chapter in Part IV walks through the current versions. The names change; the playbook doesn't.

Here's my read: COINTELPRO's real target wasn't any individual leader. It was trust. Informants, forgeries, bad-jacketing — all of it was designed to make people inside a movement suspect each other. A movement that trusts itself can survive anything on this list. A movement that doesn't will tear itself apart, and the Bureau won't have to lift a finger. Guard your internal trust like it's the treasury. It is.

The Letter They Sent to King

In November 1964, Martin Luther King Jr. received an anonymous package: a letter and tape recordings from warrantless FBI surveillance of his hotel rooms. The letter was written to look like it came from a disillusioned Black activist. It told King there was "but one way out" before he accepted his Nobel Peace Prize.

King and his aides understood exactly what it meant: the FBI was urging him to kill himself.

A copy of the letter was later found in the work files of Deputy FBI Director William C. Sullivan. The Church Committee reproduced it in Book III of its report and confirmed, from the Bureau's own files, that the FBI wrote it.

Sit with that for a second. The federal government's domestic intelligence agency tried to blackmail the country's most prominent nonviolent leader into suicide — using tapes from illegal surveillance, in a forged letter, timed to his Nobel Prize. That's not a conspiracy theory. That's the Senate's documented record.

Here's my read: they went after King psychologically because they couldn't beat him politically. When the state starts trying to break a leader's mind, it's because the movement's ideas are winning. That's the tell. It doesn't make it hurt less — but it tells you where you stand.

Fred Hampton: Two Buckets

This section gets two buckets, and they don't mix. Solemnity, not sensationalism.

Bucket one — documented:

  • FBI informant William O'Neal supplied the Bureau with a floor plan of Fred Hampton's Chicago apartment, marking where Hampton slept.
  • FBI memos discussed "neutralizing" Hampton — the same word from the 1967 Hoover directive.
  • In a pre-dawn raid on December 4, 1969, Chicago police stormed the apartment and killed Hampton — 21 years old, chairman of the Illinois Black Panther Party — in his bed, alongside fellow Panther Mark Clark.
  • An FBI crime-scene examiner testified that police fired at least 89 shots while only one shot came from inside the apartment.
  • In 1982, the city of Chicago, Cook County, and the federal government paid a $1.85 million settlement to the survivors and the families.

That is the documented record. A 21-year-old was killed in his bed in a raid the FBI helped set up with an informant's floor plan, after writing memos about "neutralizing" him, and the government paid $1.85 million rather than defend it in court.

Bucket two — not established:

  • The claim that O'Neal drugged Hampton's drink the night before the raid. It's asserted in activist accounts and some documentaries. It is not established in the documented record.
  • The stronger claim that the FBI directly ordered the killing, as opposed to enabling it through intelligence. Also not established.

I keep these buckets separate because the documented bucket is already damning, and mixing in the unproven claims gives people an excuse to dismiss all of it. The facts don't need embellishment. They need witnesses.

Hoover had named the Panthers the "greatest threat to the internal security of the country" the year before Hampton was killed. Whatever you think of the Panthers' politics, understand what that label meant in practice: it meant the full weight of the federal government, aimed at a 21-year-old in his bed.

Here's my read: Hampton's killing is the outer edge of what "they hit back" can mean. Most of you will never face anything like it. But every movement should know where the edge is, because the people who don't know the edge exists are the ones who walk past it. Know the cost. Then decide — with open eyes — what you're willing to pay.

The Union-Busting Playbook

The state has its playbook. Employers have theirs, and the book's research gives us the documented bones of it.

Start with the law, because the law is the whole game. Before 1935, employers could legally fire you for joining a union or going on strike [law since changed]. The Wagner Act — enacted July 5, 1935 — changed that: Section 7 gave workers the right to organize, bargain collectively, and engage in concerted activity, and created the National Labor Relations Board [current law]. That protection is real, but it's a floor, not a fortress — it gets tested, narrowed, and worked around constantly, and enforcement depends on who's running the Board.

From the documented record in this book's research, the employer's side of the playbook runs on a few reliable moves:

  • Fire the organizers. It was legal before 1935, and the instinct never went away — now it hides behind pretexts. The Flint strikers won an explicit promise of no reprisals in their settlement because they knew what happened to organizers who lost.
  • Starve the network. In Montgomery, carpool drivers faced tickets, bogus arrests, and cancelled insurance — pressure applied not to the leaders but to the infrastructure that made the boycott possible. Go after the dispatch stations, the drivers, the donors, the landlords. Same logic as COINTELPRO's pressure on employers and donors: strangle the support system.
  • Criminalize the action. Montgomery's leaders were indicted under a 1921 anti-boycott law. The Flint strikers defied a court injunction. Birmingham's marchers were jailed by the hundreds. The move is always the same: turn the protest into a crime, then let the legal system do the punishing.
  • Infiltrate and divide. The COINTELPRO tactics — informants, forged letters, bad-jacketing — weren't invented for unions, but the logic ports over perfectly: get inside, sow suspicion, split the leadership, provoke the hotheads. Any workplace campaign should assume the boss has ears in the room.

One honest gap: this book's research notes document the state's playbook in detail, but the modern private-sector union-busting industry — the consultants, the captive-audience meetings, the legal delay strategies — isn't in the research file. That's a hole the book's later passes should fill, because most readers will meet the employer's playbook before they ever meet the FBI's.

Here's my read: every one of these moves has the same goal — raise the personal cost of participating until participation stops. Firings, arrests, insurance cancellations: they're all just prices. The movements that survived were the ones that figured out how to share the price — strike funds, bail funds, carpool networks, mass meetings — so no one person had to pay it alone. Solidarity isn't a slogan. It's cost-sharing.

The lesson for you: plan for the retaliation before it comes. Know your rights under the NLRA [current law — but talk to a real labor lawyer, not a book]. Build the bail fund before anyone needs bail. Assume the room isn't private. And never, ever let them pick you off one at a time.

Surveillance: Then and Now

Then: wiretaps without warrants, bugs planted in break-ins, informants in the meetings, mail opened and photographed. The Church Committee documented all of it. The state had to work hard to watch you — send a man, plant a device, develop the film.

Now: you carry the listening device in your pocket, voluntarily, and charge it every night. Location history, message metadata, social graphs, facial recognition on protest footage, license-plate readers on the route to the march.

The details of the modern surveillance landscape — what's legal, what's happening anyway, and what you can actually do about it — live in Part IV, the digital chapter. I'm not duplicating it here. But the principle belongs in this chapter, because it's the through-line from COINTELPRO to today:

Here's my read: the technology changed; the purpose didn't. Then and now, surveillance serves the same function — to map the network, identify the leaders, and find the pressure points. The defense hasn't changed either: compartmentalize what needs compartmentalizing, keep your communications clean, and — most important — build a movement that doesn't collapse if any one person's phone ends up in an evidence bag. If your whole operation depends on one group chat staying secret, you don't have an operation. You have a hope.

The lesson for you: act like you're being watched, because you might be — and build like it doesn't matter. The goal was never perfect secrecy. The goal is a movement too distributed, too trusted, and too stubborn to be decapitated.

Chapter 7 — What the Numbers Say

Everything so far has been stories. Stories are how humans learn, but stories can also lie by selection — you remember the wins, you forget the losses, and you walk away thinking victory is the norm. This chapter is the antidote: the largest systematic study ever done of whether nonviolent resistance actually works, what it found, where it's weakening, and what its critics say.

Read the numbers. Then decide for yourself.

323 Campaigns: The Chenoweth–Stephan Finding

In 2008, political scientists Erica Chenoweth and Maria Stephan published "Why Civil Resistance Works: The Strategic Logic of Nonviolent Conflict" in the journal International Security (vol. 33, no. 1, pp. 7–44), later expanded into a 2011 book from Columbia University Press. It remains the landmark study in this field.

The setup: they built a dataset — NAVCO, the Nonviolent and Violent Campaigns and Outcomes dataset — covering 323 major resistance campaigns from 1900 to 2006. "Campaigns" means large-scale efforts by nonstate actors against states. "Success" has a precise definition here: the campaign achieved its stated maximalist goals — typically removing the incumbent national leadership from power, or winning territorial independence or secession. Not partial reforms. Not "raised awareness." The big prize.

The finding: primarily nonviolent campaigns succeeded 53% of the time, compared with 26% for primarily violent campaigns. Nonviolent campaigns that faced violent repression were about six times more likely to succeed than violent campaigns facing repression.

Carry the date range with those numbers everywhere they go: 1900–2006. They describe a century of history, not the present moment. More on that below.

Why does nonviolence win, according to the authors? Three mechanisms:

  1. Participation. Nonviolent action has lower barriers to entry — you don't need a gun, training, or a willingness to kill. So nonviolent campaigns get bigger and more diverse: old people, young people, workers, professionals, religious groups. Numbers are leverage.
  2. Legitimacy and backfire. Nonviolent discipline sustains the movement's moral standing, and when a regime beats peaceful people, it tends to backfire — the authors call it "political jiu-jitsu." Repression becomes the regime's own worst advertisement.
  3. Defections. Mass participation shakes the loyalty of the opponent's own pillars — including the police and military. Soldiers will fire on armed insurgents all day. Firing on unarmed grandmothers is how you get mutinies.

Here's my read: notice what's doing the work in that list. It's not niceness. It's not moral purity. It's mechanics — bigger crowds, worse optics for the regime, more defections from its enforcers. Nonviolence wins the way a lever wins: not by being virtuous, but by being better engineered. Keep that in mind when someone calls it weakness.

The Decline Since 2010: The Honest Caveat

Here's where an honest book tells you the part its own side would rather skip.

The 53%/26% figures cover 1900–2006. Chenoweth and Stephan updated the data, and the trend is not friendly. In a 2016 Washington Post update incorporating 2011–2015 data, the overall figures held roughly steady (51% vs. 27%) — but in the then-current decade, nonviolent campaigns were succeeding only 30% of the time, versus 12% for violent ones. Chenoweth's later work finds the nonviolent success rate peaked in the 1990s at around 65% and has fallen to below 34% since 2010.

Why the drop? Chenoweth points to several causes, and they're worth knowing cold:

  • Savvier state countermeasures. Regimes learned. Information control, shutting down or flooding the internet, criminalizing protest itself, and — critically — provoking violent flanks to justify crackdowns and strip movements of their nonviolent legitimacy.
  • Smaller, protest-dependent movements. More movements now rely on big street demonstrations without the deep organization underneath — no parallel institutions, no sustained economic pressure, no long-term structure. Protests are events; movements are organisms. Events are easier to wait out.
  • Fewer security-force defections. The loyalty-shift mechanism — the mutinies, the police refusing orders, the soldiers joining the crowd — is happening less. Regimes have gotten better at keeping their enforcers loyal, paid, and ideologically sealed off.

So the honest statement is this: nonviolent resistance has the best track record of any method in the 1900–2006 data, and its success rate has been declining for over a decade, and it still outperforms violent resistance in the recent data too (30% vs. 12% isn't great, but it's not close). All three of those are true at the same time. Anyone who quotes you the 53% without the date range is selling you the past. Anyone who quotes you the decline without the comparison is selling you despair.

Here's my read: the decline isn't a verdict on nonviolence — it's a scouting report on the other side. Regimes studied the same research we did, and they adapted: they learned to provoke the violent fringe, to criminalize the protest before it starts, to keep their soldiers loyal. That means the movements that win now will be the ones that adapt back — deeper organization, tighter nonviolent discipline, economic pressure that doesn't depend on a single day in the streets. The playbook in Part III is built for exactly that world.

The 3.5% Rule: An Observation, Not a Formula

You've probably heard this one: no campaign that got 3.5% of the population into sustained active participation has ever failed — except Bahrain. It's called the "3.5% rule," and it comes from Chenoweth's research.

Here's what it is: a descriptive observation, not a law of nature. Chenoweth herself stresses this. It describes what happened in the dataset. It does not guarantee what will happen next. Bahrain is the exception that proves you can't treat it as physics.

Some useful context the hype usually drops:

  • In absolute terms, 3.5% of the U.S. population is roughly 12 million people — in the streets, striking, boycotting, sustained, not for a weekend. That's an almost unimaginable number. Treat anyone who invokes it casually with suspicion.
  • Most successful campaigns never reached 3.5%. The observation is about a ceiling nobody's broken through from below, not a threshold you must hit. Plenty of wins happened with far fewer people.

So use it for what it is: a reminder that mass participation is the variable that matters most, and that no regime in the dataset survived truly massive, sustained, nonviolent defiance. Don't use it as a recruitment target or a victory formula. It isn't one.

The Critics' Corner

A serious book steelmans the objections. Here are the main ones, fairly stated:

The coding problem. Critics like Alexei Anisin argue the NAVCO binary — "primarily nonviolent" vs. "primarily violent" — is too coarse. Some campaigns coded as nonviolent successes involved unarmed or reactive violence along the way; the dataset's neat categories are messier on the ground. And by starting in 1900, the study excludes centuries of history that include many violent successes. Fair points. They don't erase the finding, but they put error bars on it.

The company you keep. Chenoweth's own research found that organized armed violence operating alongside an otherwise nonviolent movement reduces that movement's chances of success. The violent flank doesn't help — it gives the regime its excuse, fractures the coalition, and kills the defection mechanism. If your movement has people itching to escalate, this is the number to show them.

The "so what" problem. "Success" in the dataset means maximalist goals — toppling rulers, winning independence. Most of what you'll be doing — winning a union contract, stopping a development, getting a policy changed — is sub-maximalist, and the dataset's headline numbers don't directly describe those fights. The mechanisms (participation, legitimacy, defections) still apply, but don't quote 53% at your city council like it's a warranty.

Here's my read: the critics sharpen the finding rather than killing it. Yes, the categories are coarse. Yes, the date range matters. Yes, maximalist isn't your fight. And even with all of that, the pattern holds across a century and hundreds of campaigns: disciplined nonviolence beats violence by roughly two to one, and violent flanks make things worse. That's not a fragile result. That's a sturdy one with honest edges.

Here's My Read: Why This Whole Book Is Nonviolent

You've now read the history and the numbers, so let me say the thing plainly.

The nonviolence commitment in this book isn't just moral — though for the record, I think the moral case is strong, and I won't pretend otherwise. It's strategic. Across 323 campaigns over more than a century, primarily nonviolent movements succeeded 53% of the time against 26% for violent ones — and even in the declining recent data, nonviolence still outperforms violence by more than two to one. The mechanisms aren't mysterious: more people can participate, repression backfires harder, and the regime's own enforcers are likelier to defect. And Chenoweth's own data shows that adding organized violence to a nonviolent movement lowers its odds.

That's why this whole book is built on nonviolence. Not because it's pure. Not because it's safe — Chapter 6 just showed you it isn't. Because it's the strategy with the better track record, and I'm not in the business of recommending the strategy with the worse one.

One more thing, and it matters. Nonviolence in this book doesn't mean passivity, and it doesn't mean politeness. The sit-down strikers occupied GM's factories. The boycotters strangled a bus system for 381 days. Otpor mocked a dictator to his face. None of that was polite. All of it was nonviolent. There's a difference between nonviolent and nice, and the people in power count on you not knowing it.

Don't be nice. Be disciplined. Be massive. Be unmovable. The record says that's what wins.
