PART III — THE SHIELD: LAW AS A TOOL

You've spent two parts of this book learning how power works and how to move against it. This part is about something different: the weapon power left lying around because it forgot you might pick it up.

The law was written mostly by the powerful, for the powerful — no sense pretending otherwise. But every now and then, ordinary people forced concessions into it, and those concessions are still on the books. The First Amendment. Section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act. Freedom of Information laws. They are shields. Not magic, not guarantees — shields. A shield doesn't make you invincible. It makes a baton a bad bet.

Before we start, two rules, and they're not optional.

First: this is legal information, not legal advice. Law varies by state, it changes over time, and it changes for political reasons as often as legal ones. Nothing in this book substitutes for a lawyer. When you're in real trouble, or about to be, get one — legal aid organizations exist, many of them free or low-cost, and we'll keep pointing you at them. I'm not your lawyer. I'm a book.

Second: you'll see labels in these chapters, and they matter. Here's how to read them:

  • [Fact] — established, checkable, settled.
  • [Current law] — settled enough to rely on, but know your state and stay alert.
  • [Varies by state] — the law genuinely differs where you live. Look it up before you act.
  • [Unstable] — contested, in flux, or being actively rewritten. Do not build your whole plan on it.
  • Here's my read: — my analysis, my opinion. Labeled so you always know which voice you're hearing.

Keep those straight and this part will serve you. Mix them up and you'll learn the difference the hard way, in a courtroom or a cell. Don't.

Chapter 8 — Your Rights on the Street

The ground you're standing on

[Fact] The First Amendment protects speech, assembly, and petition against the government. Not against everyone. This is the single most misunderstood point in protest law, so let's get it cold: a mall owner can throw you out for your sign (in most states — a few, like California under Pruneyard, give shoppers extra speech protections on private mall property, so know your state's rules). Your employer can fire you for what you say on the job — labor law is a separate question, and we'll get to it in the next chapter. A private college campus can set its own speech rules. The Constitution is a restraint on the state, not a pass for everyplace.

But public ground is public ground. [Fact] In Hague v. CIO (1939), the Supreme Court said that streets, sidewalks, and parks "have immemorially been held in trust for the use of the public" for assembly and for communicating thoughts to one another. That sentence is almost ninety years old and it still holds: the sidewalk under your feet is one of the oldest protected spaces in American law.

[Fact] The modern map of which government property counts comes from Perry Education Assn. v. Perry Local Educators' Assn. (1983). Government property falls into three buckets:

  1. Traditional public forums — streets, sidewalks, parks. The strongest protection. The government's ability to restrict speech here is at its weakest.
  2. Designated or limited public forums — spaces the government has opened for speech, like a city auditorium rented out for meetings. Protected, but the government can set the terms of the opening.
  3. Nonpublic forums — everything else it owns that isn't for speech: a military base, a jail lobby, the inside of a government office. Speech here gets the least protection.

Here's my read: the forum doctrine is a map of where your rights are thickest. Standing on a public sidewalk with a sign? You're in the thick of it. Standing in the lobby of the police station with the same sign? Different bucket, different odds. Know which ground you're on before you act like the law has your back.

What the government can't do

[Current law] The government cannot ban or punish speech because of its viewpoint. In Police Dept. of Chicago v. Mosley (1972), the Supreme Court struck down a city ordinance that banned picketing near schools but made an exception for labor picketing. The principle is clean: the government doesn't get to pick which messages are allowed. Your sign gets the same sidewalk as the other guy's sign, no matter who runs city hall.

[Current law] Advocacy of lawbreaking is protected unless it meets the Brandenburg incitement test. From Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969): speech must be both directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and likely to incite or produce such action. Two prongs, and both have to fire. "The system is corrupt and we should rise up someday" — protected. "Burn that building down right now, here's the gas" — not. The gap between those two sentences is where most protest speech lives, and the law puts it on the protected side.

Here's my read: Brandenburg is one of the strongest sentences a court ever wrote for ordinary people. It means the government can't punish you for being angry in public, for predicting trouble, for talking about resistance in the abstract. It can only reach you when your words are a match and the gasoline is already poured. That's a high bar, and it was set high on purpose.

What the government can do

Now the other side, and don't skip it — the most dangerous rights are the ones you understand halfway.

[Current law] The government can impose content-neutral time, place, and manner restrictions. The test comes from Ward v. Rock Against Racism (1989), and it has three parts: the restriction must be (1) content-neutral — justified without reference to what's being said, (2) narrowly tailored to serve a significant governmental interest, and (3) leave open ample alternative channels for the message.

Here's the part people miss: in Ward, the Court held that the government does not have to use the least speech-restrictive means. It just has to be reasonable and neutral. So a city doesn't have to prove there was no gentler way to handle your march. It just has to prove the rule wasn't about your message.

[Current law] That means cities may lawfully require permits for marches that block streets or use amplified sound. The foundation is Cox v. New Hampshire (1941), where the Supreme Court upheld a parade permit requirement. But — and this is load-bearing — permit schemes must have clear, non-discretionary standards and cannot discriminate by viewpoint. The permit clerk doesn't get to decide whose cause is worthy. The rules have to be rules, applied to everyone, or they're unconstitutional.

The bottom line, plain: you can hold a sign on a public sidewalk without a permit in most places. The moment you want to march in the street, run a bullhorn at high volume, or camp overnight in the park, the city can lawfully require advance permission — but it must apply the rules to everyone equally, whatever the message. If the city waves one group's march through and buries yours in paperwork, that's not a permit scheme. That's viewpoint discrimination wearing a permit scheme's clothes, and Mosley says no.

Here's my read: permits are the gray zone where rights get nibbled instead of bitten. A permit rule applied fairly is the price of sharing the street. A permit rule applied selectively is censorship with a clipboard. Watch the clipboard.

Your right to record the police

[Current law — but read the limits below] As of August 2026, an overwhelming circuit-level consensus: eight sister circuits had already recognized a First Amendment right to record law enforcement officers performing their duties in public, and then the Second Circuit joined them in Massimino v. Benoit (2d Cir., Aug. 2026) — bringing the total to nine circuits: the 1st, 2d, 3d, 4th, 5th, 7th, 9th, 10th, and 11th. The key cases along the way:

  • Glik v. Cunniffe (1st Cir., 2011): openly recording police in public is protected; Simon Glik's arrest under the Massachusetts wiretap law for openly recording officers was unlawful.
  • ACLU of Illinois v. Alvarez (7th Cir., 2012): Illinois's eavesdropping statute likely unconstitutional as applied to recording on-duty police.
  • Gericke v. Begin (1st Cir., 2014): same right, on a traffic stop.
  • Fields v. Philadelphia (3d Cir., 2017): the First Amendment protects photographing, filming, or otherwise recording officers conducting their official duties in public.
  • Turner v. Driver (5th Cir., 2017): the right exists, "subject only to reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions" — though the officers in that case got qualified immunity because the right wasn't clearly established in the 5th Circuit at the time. It is now.
  • Earlier recognition in Smith v. City of Cumming (11th Cir., 2000), Fordyce v. City of Seattle (9th Cir., 1995), Sharpe v. Winterville Police Dep't (4th Cir., 2023), and Irizarry v. Yehia (10th Cir., 2022).

[Fact] That's the consensus. Now the limits, because a half-understood right is a trap:

  • You may not interfere with police activity. The camera is protected; getting in the way is not. Officers can enforce reasonable limits — staying back from an active scene, not blocking the street, not shouting over orders.
  • Reasonable time, place, and manner limits apply. Same doctrine as the protest section. The right to record isn't a right to record from two feet away in the middle of a crime scene.
  • [Varies by state] Audio and wiretapping laws differ. Some states require all parties' consent to record audio — the so-called "two-party consent" states. Openly recording video of police in public is broadly protected. Secretly recording audio where someone has a reasonable expectation of privacy is the danger zone. The 1st Circuit in Glik held that openly recording police performing public duties falls outside what the wiretap law was for — but that was Massachusetts, and your state is your state. Check your state's recording law. Say it out loud with me: check your state's recording law.
  • [Unstable — because it's unfinished] The Supreme Court has not directly ruled on this. The consensus is circuit-level — deep, broad, and persuasive, but still circuit-level. One thing it does not cover: the sources found do not establish this right in the 6th, 8th, or D.C. Circuits. Don't claim they do, and don't assume they don't. Know your circuit.

Here's my read: the camera is the poor man's bodycam — except the footage belongs to you, not the department, and it doesn't mysteriously malfunction at the interesting part. The right-to-record consensus is one of the most useful things the courts have handed ordinary people in the last twenty years. Use it. From a distance. Without interfering. And check your state's audio law first.

If you're arrested

First: getting arrested is not a victory and not a strategy. No chapter of this book romanticizes it. An arrest costs you money, time, your job maybe, and puts you in a cage with people who don't care about your cause. Know your rights so that if it happens, you don't make it worse. That's the whole spirit here.

[Fact] The Fifth Amendment protects you against compelled self-incrimination. Miranda v. Arizona (1966) requires police to warn you — before custodial interrogation, meaning you're in custody and they're questioning you — that you have the right to remain silent, that anything you say can be used against you, and that you have the right to an attorney.

The words to say, exactly:

"I am exercising my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer."

Then stop talking. To the police and to your cellmates — yes, cellmates; people in holding talk, and it gets repeated. The right is silence. Use all of it. Once you unequivocally request an attorney, interrogation has to stop until counsel is present. That's the Fifth Amendment's Miranda–Edwards rule doing its job — the Sixth Amendment's right to counsel generally attaches later, after formal proceedings begin, which is why the Miranda warning matters first.

[Current law] Don't consent to searches. The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures, and police can search without a warrant only under recognized exceptions — but consent is its own exception, and it's the one they ask for because it's the easiest. Say, clearly and calmly:

"I do not consent to this search."

Saying it doesn't physically stop an officer who searches anyway. It does something that matters later: it prevents the state from claiming in court that you agreed. The fight over the search happens in a courtroom, in front of a judge, with a lawyer. It does not happen on the curb. Do not physically resist a search. State your non-consent, stay calm, and let the court fight it.

[Current law] Don't unlock your phone. In Riley v. California (2014), the Supreme Court held unanimously that police need a warrant to search the digital contents of a cell phone seized incident to arrest. The old "search incident to arrest" exception — the one that let them go through your pockets — does not extend to the universe of data on a modern phone. The Court understood that a phone isn't a pocket. It's your whole life.

The practical rule: do not voluntarily unlock the phone, and do not hand over the passcode. [Unstable] The law around compelled passcode disclosure — whether the state can force you to give it up — is actively litigated and varies by jurisdiction. The safe, universal advice, good everywhere: don't unlock it yourself. Let Riley and a lawyer do the work.

Write the legal aid number on your arm in marker before a protest. Memorize one phone number that isn't in your phone. Tell somebody where you're going. None of that is in a Supreme Court opinion. All of it is in the wisdom of people who've been through it. Respect them.

Sources and further reading

  • Hague v. CIO, 307 U.S. 496 (1939) — streets, sidewalks, parks "held in trust" for public assembly and communication.
  • Perry Education Assn. v. Perry Local Educators' Assn., 460 U.S. 37 (1983) — the three forum categories: traditional, designated/limited, nonpublic.
  • Police Dept. of Chicago v. Mosley, 408 U.S. 92 (1972) — no viewpoint discrimination by government.
  • Brandenburg v. Ohio, 393 U.S. 104 (1969) — the incitement test: directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it.
  • Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781 (1989) — the time/place/manner test; government need not use the least-restrictive means.
  • Cox v. New Hampshire, 312 U.S. 569 (1941) — parade permits lawful with clear, non-discretionary, viewpoint-neutral standards.
  • Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir., 2011); Fields v. Philadelphia, 862 F.3d 353 (3d Cir., 2017); Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir., 2017); Massimino v. Benoit (2d Cir., Aug. 2026) — the right-to-record consensus.
  • Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966) — warnings before custodial interrogation; the right to remain silent and to counsel.
  • Riley v. California, 573 U.S. 373 (2014) — warrant required to search a phone's digital contents incident to arrest.
  • Your state's recording/wiretapping statute — look it up before you need it, not after.
  • A local legal aid organization or National Lawyers Guild chapter — find yours before the protest, not from the holding cell.

Chapter 9 — Your Rights at Work

The right you didn't know you had

[Fact] Section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act, 29 U.S.C. § 157, gives "employees" the right "to engage in... concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection." Read that phrase again: or other mutual aid or protection. It doesn't say "union members." It says employees.

Here's the part almost nobody knows: this applies to non-union workers too. It covers nearly all private-sector employees, union or not. You don't need a card, a local, or a steward. You need co-workers and a shared gripe.

[Fact] The coverage is broad but not total. Section 7 reaches nearly all private-sector employees — and excludes public-sector employees, agricultural workers, domestic workers, independent contractors, and supervisors. If you're a supervisor, or your boss has classified you as an independent contractor, the shield may not cover you — and the contractor classification is itself one of the great battlegrounds of labor law. (If you're misclassified, that's a fight worth having, with a lawyer.)

[Current law] "Concerted activity" covers: talking with co-workers about wages, benefits, and working conditions. Circulating a petition. Walking off the job over safety or conditions. Complaining to management on behalf of co-workers. Posting about workplace conditions online. The NLRB's own public summary puts it plainly: an employer may not discharge, discipline, threaten, or coercively question employees for this protected concerted activity. Even a single worker acting on behalf of others — bringing group complaints to management, trying to get co-workers to act together — can count as concerted.

Two cases built this house:

  • [Fact] NLRB v. Washington Aluminum Co., 370 U.S. 9 (1962): non-union employees walked out over freezing working conditions. The company fired them. The Supreme Court said the firing was unlawful — even a spontaneous, unorganized walkout over conditions is protected Section 7 activity. No union. No strike vote. No paperwork. Just cold workers who'd had enough, together.
  • [Fact] Eastex, Inc. v. NLRB, 437 U.S. 556 (1978): "mutual aid or protection" reaches beyond immediate collective-bargaining concerns — workers distributing a newsletter about political issues affecting them were protected. The shield is wider than the contract table.

Here's my read: Section 7 is the most underused weapon in American working life. Millions of people have been fired for things this statute protects, and never knew the statute existed. The boss counts on that. Every boss counts on that. Now you know.

The shield is real — and it's contested

[Unstable] Now the cold water, because I'd rather you hear it from me than learn it from a pink slip. NLRB doctrine swings between administrations. The Board's tests for what counts as "concerted," and how far employer work rules can go in restricting worker speech, have been rewritten by successive Boards. Remedies and enforcement posture depend on who sits on the Board and who the General Counsel is. A protection that was read broadly last year can be read narrowly this year.

[Fact] And the enforcement path matters: charges are filed with and enforced exclusively through the NLRB — an unfair-labor-practice charge, then a Board investigation, then a Board remedy. The typical remedy is reinstatement and back pay. It is not court damages. You don't get a jury and a big number. You get your job back and the wages you lost, if you win, after a process that takes time.

So present this to yourself honestly: Section 7 is a real but politically contested shield, not a settled guarantee. It's a law, enforced by humans, inside a political system. Use it — but use it with your eyes open, with documentation (more on that below), and with the understanding that the ground can shift under it.

Here's my read: a contested shield is still a shield. The people who want you to think it isn't are the same people it restrains. Don't let the perfect be the enemy of the protected.

Forming a union: the mechanics

[Current law] The traditional path to a union runs through the NLRB and looks like this:

  1. Showing of interest. To petition the NLRB for an election — an RC petition, usually filed by a union, under 29 U.S.C. § 159 — the petition needs support from at least 30% of employees in the proposed bargaining unit, typically via signed authorization cards. (That's long-standing Board procedure. We're stating the 30% rule as the rule; the exact regulatory citation isn't pinned down here and doesn't matter for your purposes.)
  2. Investigation and election. The NLRB investigates, determines an appropriate bargaining unit — who's in, who's out — and conducts a secret-ballot election.
  3. Certification. If a majority of votes cast favors the union, the Board certifies it as the exclusive bargaining representative. Note: majority of votes cast, not of everyone employed. Turnout matters. And once certified, the employer must bargain in good faith — 29 U.S.C. § 158(a)(5).

[Fact] A shortcut has always existed: voluntary recognition. An employer may always recognize a union that demonstrates majority support — typically via authorization cards, the "card check" — without any election at all. For decades, though, employers could simply refuse recognition and insist on an election, with no further obligation. That was Linden Lumber (1971), and it meant the boss could force you through the whole slow election machinery even when a clear majority had already signed cards — months of captive-audience meetings and one-on-one pressure while the clock ran.

Then came Cemex. And Cemex is where you need to watch the labels closely.

[Unstable — do not bank on this] In Cemex Construction Materials Pacific, LLC, 372 NLRB No. 130 (2023), the Biden-era Board changed the game: when a union demands recognition, the employer must either recognize the union or promptly file an RM petition — within two weeks — to test the union's claimed majority. No more just saying no and waiting. Further, if the employer commits an unfair labor practice serious enough to set aside an election, the Board will issue a bargaining order — certifying the union outright — instead of ordering a re-run election. That's a major relaxation of the old Gissel standard (NLRB v. Gissel Packing Co., 395 U.S. 575 (1969)).

Here's where it stands, and why it's flagged [Unstable]:

  • The 6th Circuit rejected the Cemex bargaining-order framework in Brown-Forman Corp. v. NLRB (6th Cir., March 6, 2026) — returning to Gissel in the Sixth Circuit's states: Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee.
  • The 9th Circuit affirmed the underlying Cemex bargaining orders under Gissel in April 2026 but deliberately declined to rule on whether the Cemex framework itself is valid. A sidestep, not an endorsement.
  • The framework is contested and subject to further change: the current Republican-majority Board may revisit Cemex once it regains a full quorum, and courts are still sorting out which parts survive.

Here's my read: Cemex is the best thing to happen to union organizing in fifty years, and it's contested — a future Board or court could narrow it or overturn it. That's not a reason to ignore it — it's a reason to move while the law is favorable and to build majorities so solid they don't depend on which way the Board leans. Organize like the friendly rules expire tomorrow. They might.

The practical part: organizing where you work

Law is the shield. Organizing is the arm that holds it. Here's the work, step by step.

Build an organizing committee first. Not a mass meeting — a small group. Find the two or three co-workers everyone trusts: the person who trains the new hires, the one who's been there longest, the one people complain to. Meet off-site, off company devices, off company time. The committee's job is to map the workplace: who works where, who influences whom, what the issues are, who's with you, who's scared, who's the boss's ear.

The one-on-one conversation. This is the atom of all organizing. Not a speech — a conversation. Here's a script. Adapt it to your mouth:

"Hey — can I ask you something? How are you feeling about [the schedule / the pay / the safety thing / whatever the live issue is]? ... Yeah, me too. I've been talking to a few people, and a lot of us feel the same way. Nobody's saying we have to do anything big. But what if we wrote it down — all of us who feel this way — and asked for a meeting about it? Would you be willing to talk more? No pressure, and this stays between us."

That's it. Listen more than you talk. The question does the work. The classic organizer's rule: never lead with the union. Lead with the issue. The union is the answer to a question the worker has to ask first.

Document retaliation like your job depends on it — because it does. The moment you start organizing, start a paper trail. Not on company devices, not on company email, not on the work Slack:

  1. Dates, times, places. Every meeting, every conversation with management, every schedule change, every write-up. Write it down the same day.
  2. Witnesses. Who was present? Get names. Ask them, privately, to write down what they saw too.
  3. Keep copies off-site. Photos of schedules, screenshots of messages, copies of write-ups — saved to a personal device or a personal cloud account the company can't touch.
  4. The timeline is the weapon. Retaliation cases are won on timing: you engaged in protected activity on Tuesday, you got written up on Thursday for something nobody's ever been written up for. A clean timeline turns "performance issue" into "pretext," and pretext is what the NLRB looks for.
  5. File fast. If you're fired or disciplined for organizing, file an unfair-labor-practice charge with the NLRB promptly. There are time limits. Don't sit on it hoping things blow over.

Here's my read: the company will have lawyers, consultants, and a playbook. Your playbook is older: each other, a timeline, and a statute that says you have the right to act together. It's not a fair fight. It never was. Organize anyway.

Sources and further reading

  • National Labor Relations Act, Section 7 — 29 U.S.C. § 157 (concerted activities for "mutual aid or protection"); Section 9 — 29 U.S.C. § 159 (election petitions); Section 8(a)(5) — 29 U.S.C. § 158(a)(5) (duty to bargain in good faith).
  • NLRB v. Washington Aluminum Co., 370 U.S. 9 (1962) — non-union spontaneous walkout over conditions, protected.
  • Eastex, Inc. v. NLRB, 437 U.S. 556 (1978) — "mutual aid or protection" beyond immediate bargaining.
  • Cemex Construction Materials Pacific, LLC, 372 NLRB No. 130 (2023) — recognize-or-petition within two weeks; relaxed bargaining-order standard. Contested — see below.
  • Brown-Forman Corp. v. NLRB (6th Cir., Mar. 6, 2026) — rejected the Cemex bargaining-order framework in KY, MI, OH, TN.
  • The NLRB's public guidance on protected concerted activity — read the Board's own plain-language summary of your Section 7 rights.
  • A labor lawyer or a union organizer in your industry — the committee is the start, but experienced help is worth more than any book.

Chapter 10 — Your Rights as a Tenant

Stop. Read this box first.

[Varies by state — enormously] Whether you can legally withhold rent, and what happens if you do, varies enormously by state and sometimes by city. In many states, nonpayment of rent is straightforward grounds for eviction, and a "rent strike" can get participants evicted — home lost, record marked, done.

Rent withholding done correctly under a specific state statute is a different animal from a coordinated rent strike. Organizers need to know which one they're doing, because the law treats them very differently. Check your state's law before you act on anything in this chapter.

And the caveat, repeated because the stakes are a roof: this is legal information, not legal advice. Talk to a lawyer — a tenant attorney or your local legal aid office — before you withhold a dollar. The wrong move here doesn't cost you a fine. It costs you your home.

What the law actually gives you

Your landlord-tenant law is a state statute, not a vibe. Two states' versions are verified here so you can see what a real shield looks like — and what it demands of you.

Ohio — the escrow procedure. [Current law — Ohio] Ohio Rev. Code § 5321.07 gives a tenant who is current on rent a precise, step-by-step tool when the landlord won't fix habitability or code violations:

  1. Give the landlord written notice of the violations.
  2. Allow a reasonable time to fix them.
  3. If the landlord still doesn't act, deposit your rent with the court — escrow — instead of paying the landlord, until the repairs are made.

Read the shape of that: you don't stop paying. You pay the court. The money is there, the landlord just can't touch it until they do their job. And the statutory steps must be followed exactly — written notice, staying current on rent, paying into the court. Skip a step and you're not using the shield anymore; you're just a tenant who didn't pay rent, and the law knows what to do with those.

New York — the warranty of habitability. [Current law — New York] New York Real Property Law § 235-b implies a warranty of habitability into every residential lease. Implied means it's there whether the lease mentions it or not, and it cannot be waived — your landlord can't contract their way out of it with a clause you signed at move-in.

A tenant may sue for a rent reduction and may withhold rent over habitability breaches. But here's the catch, and it's a big one: the landlord can then sue for nonpayment, and the tenant must defend and countersue on the warranty. Withholding without a solid habitability claim is risky — you're betting your defense holds up in front of a judge. Legal-aid sources advise consulting a tenant attorney first. Take that advice. It's free or close to it, and the alternative is gambling with your apartment.

[Fact] What we are not doing in this book: reproducing a state-by-state rent-withholding list. Commercial compilations of "which states allow rent withholding" exist, but they're third-party roundups, not legal authority, and they go stale. Only Ohio and New York were verified to statute level here. For your state: legal aid, tenant organization, tenant attorney. That's the list.

The rent strike: respect the risk

Here's my read, plainly: tenant unions exist and organize across the country, and collective action — demands, escrow filings, court action, public pressure — has a real history of winning repairs, stopping evictions, and humbling slumlords. Organizing your building is good. Knowing your neighbors is good. Acting together is the whole thesis of this book.

But a rent strike — coordinated nonpayment — is high-risk, and I won't dress it up. Even in states with escrow statutes, the escrow route requires following the statutory steps exactly: written notice, staying current, paying into the court. Participants who simply stop paying can be evicted. The landlord's remedy for nonpayment is the oldest and sharpest tool in this whole area of law, and it does not care about your solidarity.

The shield is the statute, not the strike. If your state gives you an escrow procedure, a repair-and-deduct right, or a warranty you can sue on — use it, collectively, loudly, with every tenant in the building filing together. That's collective action inside the law's protection. A strike outside the statute is collective action outside the law's protection, and the people who can least afford to lose their housing are the ones who'd lose it first.

Here's my read: landlords count on tenants not knowing the statute exists, not talking to each other, and not calling legal aid. The most dangerous thing in this chapter isn't withholding rent — it's a building full of tenants who've all read the law, all documented the violations, and all filed on the same day. That's the move. Organized, documented, inside the statute.

Practical steps, wherever you live:

  1. Document everything. Dates, photos of the violations, copies of every written complaint to the landlord, the landlord's responses or silence. A folder — physical or digital — per apartment.
  2. Talk to your neighbors. The tenant in 3B with the same leak is not a stranger; they're your bargaining unit. Organize the building before you fight the landlord.
  3. Call legal aid first. Before withholding anything, before signing anything, before announcing anything. Most cities have a tenant legal aid office or hotline. Use it.
  4. Follow the statutory steps exactly. If your state has an escrow or notice procedure, treat it like a recipe — every step, in order, documented.
  5. Find your local tenant union or tenant organization. They've done this before. You haven't. Learn from people with scar tissue.

Sources and further reading

  • Ohio Rev. Code § 5321.07 — the rent-escrow procedure: written notice, reasonable time, deposit rent with the court.
  • New York Real Property Law § 235-b — implied warranty of habitability; cannot be waived; basis for rent-reduction suits and withholding defenses.
  • Ohio legal-aid rent-escrow guidance (e.g., Legal Aid of Western Ohio materials) — the procedure in plain language.
  • Your state's landlord-tenant statute — find it, read the habitability and escrow sections, then call legal aid to confirm you understood it right.
  • Your local legal aid office and tenant union — the two phone numbers that matter more than anything in this chapter.

Chapter 11 — Paper Weapons

FOIA: making the government show its work

[Fact] The Freedom of Information Act, 5 U.S.C. § 552, gives any person the right to request records from federal agencies. Not citizens — any person. You don't need a reason, a lawyer, or a press badge. You need a question and a stamp.

[Current law] The mechanics:

  • Agencies must respond within 20 business days — 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(6)(A). In practice this deadline is routinely missed; agencies are backlogged and slow. But it's the law, and the law is leverage: a missed deadline is the start of an appeal, and an appeal is the start of a lawsuit, and agencies know it.
  • Fee waivers are available when "disclosure of the information is in the public interest because it is likely to contribute significantly to public understanding of the operations or activities of the government and is not primarily in the commercial interest of the requester" — 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(A)(iii). Read that as: if you're digging for the public and publishing what you find, say so, and the fees should be waived or reduced. Journalists, nonprofits, and organizers invoke this routinely.
  • There are nine exemptions — national security, law enforcement, personal privacy, and others. Agencies will cite them. Some citations are legitimate; some are reflexive. Denials can be administratively appealed, and then litigated in federal court.

How to file one — the actual steps:

  1. Figure out what to ask for. Not "everything about surveillance" — that's a denial with extra steps. Ask for specific records: "all emails between [office] and [contractor] regarding [program] from [date] to [date]"; "the contract and statements of work for [system]"; "use logs," "policies," "training materials." Narrow beats broad. Records have names; learn the names.
  2. Find where to send it. Every federal agency has a FOIA office and a FOIA contact — usually listed on the agency's website under "FOIA." Send it there. If you're not sure which agency holds the records, file with your best guess — the agency will usually route it to the right office within that agency, or tell you where to go. (Don't count on one agency forwarding your request to a different agency for you.)
  3. Write it plainly. "Pursuant to the Freedom of Information Act, 5 U.S.C. § 552, I request the following records: ..." List them. Then add: "I request a waiver of fees under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(A)(iii) on the grounds that disclosure is in the public interest because [you will publish the results / you are researching for public education / etc.] and is not primarily in my commercial interest." Include your contact info. Date it. Keep a copy.
  4. Track it and follow up. You'll get a tracking number. When the 20 business days pass — and they will — follow up in writing. Then appeal. Then, if it matters enough, sue. Most requesters never get past step one of pushing back, which is exactly what the backlog counts on.
  5. Use MuckRock. MuckRock (muckrock.com) files, tracks, and publishes FOIA and state records requests. Filing through it means your request and the responsive documents become public — which, note, also strengthens the public-interest argument for your fee waiver. You're not just requesting for yourself; you're building a public archive.

[Varies by state] Every state has its own public-records law with its own deadlines, fees, and exemptions. New York's Freedom of Information Law (FOIL), for example, requires an agency response within 5 business days. Your state's law is different — look it up, and use it. Some of the most useful records for local organizing — police department policies, city contracts, emails — live at the state and local level, not the federal one.

[Fact] This isn't theory. FOIA requests have forced real disclosures:

  • The ACLU's FOIA lawsuit against the FBI, filed in 2019, produced thousands of pages in 2023 revealing the Bureau's deep involvement with the IARPA-funded Janus facial-recognition program — later folded into a multi-agency tool called Horus — including testing on footage from public surveillance cameras. Your face, on a public street, in a federal test set. Disclosed because somebody filed paperwork.
  • ACLU FOIA requests exposed federal nondisclosure agreements instructing local police to conceal their use of Stingray cell-site simulators — devices that mimic cell towers to track phones — in court filings. The government told local cops to hide the tool from judges. The paper trail proved it.

Here's my read: FOIA is slow, boring, and bureaucratic — which is exactly why it's powerful. Nobody guards against the patient. A request filed today is a disclosure in two years that changes a city council vote. The powerful classify; the persistent declassify. Be persistent.

Jury nullification: the power and the line

This section needs care, so here's the doctrine first, clean and sharp.

[Fact] Jurors have the power to acquit a defendant even when the evidence proves guilt under the law as the judge explained it. Why? Because a criminal acquittal is final — it cannot be appealed, overturned, or punished. The power exists as a matter of brute legal fact: twelve people say "not guilty," and the case is over.

[Fact] But courts do not recognize a right to be told about that power. Power versus right — keep them separate, because the whole section turns on it.

The history:

  • [Fact] Bushell's Case (1670, English Court of Common Pleas): the juror Edward Bushell was imprisoned for refusing to convict William Penn and William Mead. The court freed him, establishing that jurors cannot be punished for their verdicts — the foundation of jury independence in Anglo-American law. Three and a half centuries old, still load-bearing.
  • [Fact] Sparf v. United States (1895, Supreme Court, 5–4, Justice Harlan): federal judges are not required to inform jurors of any power to judge the law. The Court acknowledged juries "have the physical power to disregard the law, as laid down to them by the court" — but denied they have the "moral right" to do so. Since Sparf, American judges do not instruct juries on nullification. The power is universally acknowledged, even by the Sparf dissent, which stressed that acquittals are final. The instruction is universally withheld.
  • [Fact] The Fully Informed Jury Association (FIJA) — fija.org — is the long-standing organization advocating juror education on this power.

Here's my read: the system built a door, locked it, and then made it illegal for the judge to mention the door — while leaving the door itself wide open, because an acquittal can't be appealed. That's not an accident. That's the founders' compromise with mercy, frozen in amber. Know the door is there. Know you're not allowed to be told about it in the box.

Now the line — and this is presented as information, not encouragement, because the real-world record is mixed and I won't sand the edges off it:

  • [Fact] Keith Wood (Big Rapids, Michigan, 2015): arrested for handing out FIJA pamphlets on a public sidewalk outside a courthouse. Convicted in 2017 of misdemeanor "attempting to influence a jury." Sentenced to eight weekends in jail plus probation. For pamphlets. On a sidewalk.
  • [Fact] Mark Iannicelli (Denver, Colorado, 2015): charged with seven felony counts of jury tampering for handing out nullification pamphlets outside the Lindsey-Flanigan Courthouse. The charges were dismissed by the trial court, and the dismissal was affirmed on appeal. Same act, opposite outcome — different state, different judge, different day.
  • [Fact] Michael Picard (Bronx, New York, 2017): arrested for distributing jury-nullification literature. He challenged N.Y. Penal Law § 215.50(7), which bars conduct "concerning the conduct of a trial" within 200 feet of a courthouse. The Second Circuit reinstated the statute in Picard v. Magliano (2024), holding it could serve a compelling state interest. Translation: courthouse buffer-zone laws against this kind of advocacy have survived First Amendment challenge.
  • [Fact] A Florida chief judge issued an administrative order banning nullification pamphleteering at the Orange and Osceola county courthouses.

So the honest summary, with nothing hidden: the doctrine exists, the power exists, and activism near courthouses has drawn arrests with mixed legal outcomes — one man jailed, one's charges thrown out, one's constitutional challenge lost, one judge's blanket ban standing. Do not read this section as a safety verdict on pamphleteering. There isn't one. There is a power, a line, and a record. Now you know all three.

Here's my read: nullification is the system's last-resort pressure valve — the moment when twelve ordinary people can look at a law, look at a defendant, and refuse. The powerful fear it precisely because they can't appeal it. That's why the instruction is withheld and the pamphleteers get arrested. A power they can't take from you, only keep you from hearing about. So now you've heard about it.

Sources and further reading

  • The Freedom of Information Act — 5 U.S.C. § 552; 20-business-day response (§ 552(a)(6)(A)); public-interest fee waiver (§ 552(a)(4)(A)(iii)).
  • MuckRock (muckrock.com) — file, track, and publish FOIA and state records requests.
  • Your state's public-records law (e.g., New York's Freedom of Information Law, N.Y. Public Officers Law §§ 84–90) — deadlines, fees, and exemptions differ; look yours up.
  • ACLU FOIA litigation on the FBI's Janus/Horus facial-recognition involvement (disclosures 2023) and on Stingray nondisclosure agreements — documented examples of what requests can force into the open.
  • Bushell's Case (1670) — jurors cannot be punished for their verdicts.
  • Sparf v. United States, 156 U.S. 51 (1895) — judges not required to inform jurors of nullification power; power acknowledged, "moral right" denied.
  • Picard v. Magliano (2d Cir., 2024) — courthouse buffer-zone restrictions on nullification advocacy upheld.
  • The Fully Informed Jury Association — fija.org — the doctrine, the history, and the ongoing legal landscape.
  • A lawyer — before you act on any of this near a courthouse. I mean it.

Carrying the shield

That's the part. Four chapters, one idea: the law is not justice, but it is a tool, and tools don't care who picks them up.

A few things to carry with you:

Rights are muscles, not monuments. They don't protect you by existing. They protect you when they're exercised — by people who know them, in numbers, with documentation, in daylight. Every right in these four chapters was won by somebody using it before it was safe, and kept by somebody using it after it was.

The shield has edges. Every one of these protections has limits, exceptions, and jurisdictions where it runs thin. You read the labels — [Fact], [Current law], [Varies by state], [Unstable] — so you know exactly how much weight each one can bear. Respect the edges. A shield you lean on past its edge gets you hurt.

Paper trails beat speeches. The camera footage, the dated notes, the filed FOIA, the escrow receipt, the authorization cards — the unglamorous paperwork is what turns a right from a paragraph in a book into a fact in a courtroom. Be boring. Be meticulous. Be the person with the folder.

And get the lawyer. I said it in the opener and I'll say it at the close: this was information, not advice. When it's real — an arrest, a firing, an eviction notice, a subpoena — you want a professional in your corner, not a book. Legal aid is free. The National Lawyers Guild runs legal observer and hotline programs. Find yours before you need them.

The powerful wrote most of these laws. Then ordinary people bled concessions into them. The concessions are yours. Pick up the shield.

PART IV — THE ARSENAL: WHAT YOU CAN BUILD

Chapters 12–13

Everything before this was diagnosis: how power works, what it does to people like us, how it keeps us tired and divided. This part is the toolkit. Not theories — things people have actually built and actually used, with the receipts. Feed each other, hit the wallet, protect your communications, build institutions that answer to you. Pick one and start this week. The arsenal doesn't work from the shelf.

Chapter 12 — Feed Each Other

Nobody is coming to save you. That's not cynicism; it's the whole reason this chapter exists.

When the storm hits, when the jobs dry up, when the kids are hungry and the agencies have a waiting list — somebody feeds somebody. It's never the government first. It's always a neighbor. The question isn't whether people take care of each other. They do, every single time. The question is whether you build something out of it, or just survive the week and forget by spring.

This chapter is about mutual aid: ordinary people feeding, sheltering, and patching up other ordinary people, organized on purpose. Not charity — charity has a donor and a recipient, a giver and a receiver, and that power gap never goes away. Mutual aid is different. It runs on a simple idea: solidarity, not charity. Today's giver is tomorrow's receiver. You feed your people because they're your people, and when it's your turn to be hungry, they feed you.

There's a community-fridge organizer in the Midwest named Thadeaus Umpster who put it like this: "This isn't about rich people giving to poor people to assuage their guilt. Me sharing food isn't charity because these are my people." That's the whole doctrine in one sentence.

It works. And it has a long, well-documented history in this country — some of it glorious, some of it infiltrated, all of it instructive.

The Panthers Fed the Kids

In January 1969, at St. Augustine's Episcopal Church in Oakland, California, the Black Panther Party launched the Free Breakfast for Children Program. The church's rector, Father Earl Neil, and a volunteer named Ruth Beckford-Smith ran it. Eleven children ate on day one. By the end of that first week, it was 135.

That's a fact worth sitting with: 11 to 135 in five days. Not because somebody bought ad space. Because hungry kids live in every poor neighborhood in America, and when somebody starts feeding them for free, word gets around.

The program spread across the country and ran from 1969 to 1980. How many kids did it feed? You'll see the number 20,000 children a day everywhere. Here's the labeling rule working: that number comes from the Panthers themselves. It was the Party's self-report, and it was never independently audited. The exact reach is debated by historians. Say it that way and you're telling the truth; drop the caveat and you're passing along a press release as fact. Small discipline, big difference.

Now here's the part they don't teach in school. The federal government didn't just watch this happen — it targeted the breakfast program as a threat. This is documented, not a conspiracy theory:

  • In September 1968, FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover described the Panthers as "the greatest threat to the internal security of the country."
  • The Panthers were added as COINTELPRO targets that same month. (COINTELPRO ran from 1956 to 1971; it was exposed by the 1971 break-in at an FBI office in Media, Pennsylvania, and its scope was confirmed by the Church Committee in 1975–76. All of this is in the official record.)
  • In early 1969, Hoover issued a directive to "eradicate" the Panthers' "serve the people" programs — the free breakfasts, the free clinics.
  • Then, on May 15, 1969, Hoover wrote an internal memo that is worth reading word for word: "The Breakfast for Children Program represents the best and most influential activity going for the BPP and, as such, is potentially the greatest threat to efforts by authorities to neutralize the BPP and destroy what it stands for."

Read that again. The FBI director looked at a program feeding hungry children and called it a threat — not because it was violent, but because it was popular. The Panthers were winning people's loyalty by feeding them, and that was the problem. In a separate 1969 memo, Hoover told his San Francisco agents to attack the breakfast program to keep the Party "isolated from the moderate black and white community which may support it."

The campaign went beyond memos. On September 8, 1969, armed police raided the breakfast program in Watts, Los Angeles.

Here's my read: the government did not fear the Panthers because they were armed — plenty of people in America are armed and the FBI doesn't write frantic memos about them. It feared them because feeding kids is the kind of power that can't be argued with. You can demonize a gunman. You can't demonize a breakfast. So they tried anyway. That tells you something about what mutual aid actually is: not charity, but a rival power base. When you feed your own people, you become less dependent on the institutions that control you — and the institutions notice.

One thing I won't tell you: there's a popular story that the Panther breakfast program directly caused the federal School Breakfast Program (permanently authorized in 1975). You'll see it in memes and even some articles. The causal claim isn't verified in the sources, so it stays out of this book. The Panthers deserve their real history, not an inflated one.

Katrina: When the State Fled, the People Stayed

Hurricane Katrina made landfall on August 29, 2005. The levees broke. New Orleans drowned. And the response from official America was — put politely — not impressive. Superdome, Convention Center, FEMA trailers months late: you remember.

Here's what else happened, in a neighborhood called Algiers, across the river from the worst of it. On September 5, 2005 — seven days after landfall — a local organizer named Malik Rahim (a former Black Panther), a Texas anarchist organizer named Scott Crow, and an Algiers resident named Sharon Johnson founded Common Ground Relief. Four days later, on September 9, they had a first-aid station running.

What followed was one of the largest volunteer efforts in American disaster history:

  • Seven distribution centers for food, water, and supplies.
  • The Common Ground Health Clinic, which later became its own 501(c)(3).
  • A legal clinic for people tangled in FEMA bureaucracy and insurance fights.
  • Over 1,000 houses gutted — mostly in the Upper and Lower Ninth Ward — stripped to the studs so mold didn't condemn them permanently.
  • 13,000+ volunteers cycled through the organization, per an academic study by Rachel Luft.
  • The collective itself said it served 500,000+ people through its feeding stations, clinics, and rebuilding work. That's the collective's own number — take it the way you'd take the Panthers' 20,000. It's their count, and it reflects real scale even if no auditor checked it.

Now the ugly part, because this book doesn't skip the ugly parts. One of the co-founders, Brandon Darby — he arrived with the early EMT teams and served as Director of Operations from January to April 2007 — later turned out to be an FBI informant. Wikipedia dates his informing to November 2007; he infiltrated groups planning protests at the 2008 Republican National Convention in St. Paul, and his information led to the arrests of David McKay and Bradley Crowder. Malik Rahim went on Democracy Now! and said he was "heartbroken" at the revelation. That's his exact word: heartbroken.

Here's the labeling, carefully: the start date is contested. One account (Occupy.com) calls the details "murky" and says Darby may have been feeding the FBI information as early as early 2007. So: what happened at Common Ground is established; the exact timeline of his informing is disputed. Hold both categories in your head at once.

Here's my read on what the Common Ground story teaches: Katrina showed the state failing people in a crisis — that's the documented case — while neighbors saved each other — also documented. But movements get infiltrated, and the infiltrator often arrives looking like the most dedicated person in the room. Common Ground did real, massive good with an informant sitting in leadership. The work was still the work. Be honest about who you're organizing with, don't hand one person the keys to everything, and keep building anyway.

The Pandemic Pods

COVID did something strange: it made mutual aid go viral — in the literal sense and the internet sense. Neighborhood pods sprang up in nearly every state. The structure was the same everywhere: decentralized, horizontal, no headquarters, no grant applications. People matched needs to resources on group chats and spreadsheets. Rides to testing sites. Grocery runs for elders. Rent money pooled in a pinch.

Scale: roughly 50 mutual aid groups documented at the start of the pandemic, growing to 800+ by May 2020 in nearly every U.S. state. A couple of examples to make it concrete:

  • The Astoria Mutual Aid Network in Queens, New York — over 2,000 members, with the motto "Neighbors give help. Neighbors get help."
  • Mutual Aid Eastie in Boston, organized by block captains, delivering up to 5,000 meals a week at the peak.

Then came the community fridges. In February 2020, a Brooklyn anarchist mutual aid network called "A New World In Our Hearts" left a free Craigslist fridge outside a building with a "Free Food" sign. Take food, leave food. The idea predates them — the Freedge network dates to 2014 — but that fridge went viral and the model exploded. By 2022 there were 100+ community fridges across New York City.

And bail funds — same family, different front. The idea is old: the ACLU set up a national bail fund in 1920, and the Civil Rights Congress raised bail money for political defendants in the 1960s and '70s. But it scaled fast after 2020: from about a dozen community bail funds in 2015 to 100+ after 2020, per the National Bail Fund Network. The Bail Project's revolving fund ran about 30 sites in 20 states and helped release 30,000+ people — getting people out of jail so they could keep their jobs, their kids, their housing while they waited for trial.

Honesty requires the other half: after 2020, bail funds faced legislative backlash in multiple states, and New York rolled back parts of its bail reforms. That's the pattern in this whole book — you build something, it works, and somebody tries to shut it down. The backlash is evidence the thing had power, not evidence it failed.

DO THIS: Start a Mutual Aid Pod

Enough history. Here's the practical part. If you want to start something in your neighborhood — a food box, a ride list, a group that actually shows up — here's how, in five steps.

Step 1: Who's your "you people"? Pick a geography you can walk across in half an hour — your block, your building, your street, your apartment complex. Mutual aid dies when it gets abstract. "The community" is too big. Your block is real. Ten to thirty households is plenty to start.

Step 2: Name one real need. Don't start with a mission statement. Start with a need somebody actually has right now. Too many groceries going to waste? An elder who needs rides to the doctor? Kids who need after-school snacks? Parents who need emergency childcare coverage? Pick ONE. The pod that tries to do everything does nothing. You can add more later — you'll be shocked how fast it grows once it exists.

Step 3: Find your first five people. You don't need a crowd; you need five people who will show up. Knock on doors. Yes, actually knock. Post in the building group chat, the neighborhood Facebook group, the local bulletin board at the laundromat or the bodega. Say exactly this: "I'm starting a neighborhood mutual aid group — we help each other out with [the need]. Want in?" That's it. No jargon. People either want in or they don't.

Step 4: Hold one meeting, keep it short. One hour, max. Someone's kitchen, the church basement, a picnic table. The agenda is four questions: What do we need? What do we have? Who can do what? When do we start? End the meeting with one concrete thing on the calendar. A meeting that produces nothing produces nothing twice and then nobody comes back.

Step 5: Do one simple, real thing. A food box at a neighbor's porch. A shared ride list pinned in the group chat. A "who needs what / who has what" thread every Sunday. Keep it small and keep it real — one working thing beats ten planned things. And say the framing out loud, early: this is solidarity, not charity. Everybody gives, everybody receives. No saviors, no saved. The day you treat people like recipients, you've built a charity with a guilt complex instead of a pod with a backbone.

A few hard-won rules from the groups that survived:

  • Write nothing down that you wouldn't want read aloud in court. Paranoia isn't required; basic sense is.
  • Don't let one person hold everything — the money, the passwords, the relationships. Common Ground taught that one.
  • Document your work for yourselves — photos, lists, receipts — because when it's time to tell your story, you'll want your own records, not someone else's version.
  • Feed people before you lecture them. The Panthers understood this. A hungry person at your meeting is your best advertisement for whatever comes next.

Costs, honestly: this will take your time, some of your money, and occasionally your comfort. Neighbors will disappoint you. Volunteers will flake. Somebody will take more than they give for a while. None of that means it failed. It means it's real.

Sources and further reading

  • BlackPast.org — "Black Panther Party's Free Breakfast Program (1969–1980)" and "Black Panther Party's Free Medical Clinics (1969–1975)": the cleanest fact-sheets on the Panthers' serve-the-people programs.
  • Joshua Bloom et al., Black Against Empire (UC Press, 2013) — the academic history behind the FBI's targeting of the breakfast program.
  • The Church Committee reports (1975–76) and the FBI's own 1976 internal report on COINTELPRO — the government's own paper trail.
  • Rachel Luft, "Looking for Common Ground" (Narrative Works / Mutual Aid Disaster Relief) — the academic study behind the Common Ground numbers.
  • Democracy Now! interviews with Malik Rahim (2005–2008) — firsthand account, including his reaction to the Brandon Darby revelation.
  • NPR / The Public's Radio reporting (2025) on the National Bail Fund Network — the bail-fund scale numbers and the post-2020 backlash.
  • EFF's Surveillance Self-Defense (ssd.eff.org) — before you put anything in a group chat, read this. (More on this in a later chapter.)

Chapter 13 — Hit the Wallet

Power doesn't listen to speeches. It listens to money. Every person in a suit will tell you this if you buy them enough drinks: the fastest way to get a meeting with anyone is to threaten the thing they measure themselves by. For a bus company, that's fares. For a grower, that's shipments. For a university endowment, that's the portfolio. For a bank, that's deposits.

This chapter is about economic pressure — boycotts, divestment, debt refusal, and building your own institutions so you stop feeding the beast. All nonviolent. All proven. And all honest about what they can and can't do.

One note before we start: you'll notice I don't quote a lot of dollar figures for "how much money they lost." That's deliberate. Economic-damage numbers from boycotts are some of the most inflated statistics in activism — everybody remembers the round million, nobody has the ledger. Where the numbers are solid, I'll give them. Where they're commonly cited but shaky, I'll say so. The strategy doesn't need the inflation; it works without it.

Montgomery: The Bus Company Goes Broke Slowly

Chapter 5 told the full story — 381 days, the carpool network, Browder v. Gayle ending it. Here's the template, because everything in this chapter is a variation on it:

They identified the revenue stream (bus fares), organized the community to withhold it (the boycott), built the support system to make withholding sustainable for over a year (church-based carpools, Black taxi drivers charging the ten-cent fare, mass walking — with no cell phones, no apps, no group chats; just organization and stubbornness), and named the victory condition (desegregation). One honest discipline: you'll see big round numbers about the bus company's lost revenue and ridership drops — those show up in municipal fact sheets and secondary accounts but aren't traceable to primary sources. Treat them as commonly-cited estimates, not verified numbers. The documented fact is the strategy, and it worked without the inflation.

The Grapes: Starve the Supply Chain

The full history is in Chapter 5 — Filipino farmworkers walking out in Delano in September 1965, the UFW formed in 1966, the contracts signed July 29, 1970. Here's the weapon anatomy, the part this chapter is actually about:

Huerta's key move was aiming the boycott two steps down the supply chain: not just the grapes, but the grocery chains that sold the grapes. That's the sophistication. The growers could absorb a picket line. They couldn't absorb Safeway and A&P getting picketed by suburban housewives. By the end of 1969, grape shipments from California were down by up to 43% in some cities — and the pressure reached the growers through their buyers.

Five years from strike to contract. Five years of not buying grapes. That's the part nobody glamorizes: boycotts are boring. They're a million tiny refusals, sustained past the point where anyone thinks they're working. The growers thought the boycott would fizzle in months. It didn't. That gap between "this will never work" and "we sign on July 29" is where the power lives.

Divestment: Make Apartheid Unprofitable

Chapter 5 gave you the history of this campaign; here's the weapon. In April 1985, students at Columbia University started building shantytowns on campus — mock shacks to dramatize South African apartheid — and the tactic spread like fire. Cornell built the first encampments. Soon close to 50 universities had encampments and 150+ had protests. The demand: divest — sell every stock, bond, and holding connected to apartheid South Africa.

The money moved. The University of California system divested $3.1 billion in July 1986. The state of California divested $11 billion the next month. By the end of the 1980s, roughly 150 universities had fully divested.

And Congress followed the campuses. The Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986 — introduced by Representative Ron Dellums — banned new U.S. investment in South Africa, sales to its police and military, new bank loans, and imports of steel, coal, uranium, textiles, and agricultural goods. President Ronald Reagan vetoed it. The House overrode him 313–83, and the Republican-controlled Senate overrode 78–21 on October 2, 1986 — the first veto override of Reagan's presidency.

Now the honesty part, because this is where a lot of tellings get sloppy: the extent to which the divestment movement caused the fall of apartheid is debated by historians. Sanctions and divestment were real pressures — real money moved, real laws passed — but apartheid fell for many reasons, including decades of internal resistance by Black South Africans. If anyone tells you American students ended apartheid, that's a fairy tale. If anyone tells you divestment did nothing, that's also wrong. The truth is in the middle: it was a contributing pressure, not the sole cause. The lesson isn't "divestment topples regimes." The lesson is "coordinated economic pressure forces concessions from people who swore they'd never concede" — which is plenty.

The Debt Strike: Refusing to Pay Together

Here's a newer weapon, and it's elegant. What if debtors organized the way workers do — not as individual deadbeats to be shamed, but as a bloc that can bargain?

That's the Debt Collective, an offshoot of Occupy Wall Street (via the Strike Debt and Rolling Jubilee projects). The idea is collective bargaining applied to debt: one person refusing to pay is a delinquent; a thousand refusing together is a negotiating position.

The proof of concept: in February 2015, fifteen former students of the Corinthian Colleges chain — for-profit schools that had saddled students with federal loans and then collapsed — publicly refused to repay. The "Corinthian 15" grew to 200, then to a 1,000+ person cohort including former ITT Tech students.

Their legal lever was a provision almost nobody knew existed: "Defense to Repayment" (Borrower Defense) in the Higher Education Act — enacted in 1995, used only a handful of times in two decades. It says, roughly: if your school defrauded you, you can challenge the debt. The Debt Collective built an online tool letting students file those challenges with the Department of Education — turning an obscure legal footnote into a mass-action weapon.

Results: Corinthian collapsed in 2015 (about 16,000 students displaced when the doors shut). The Obama administration approved thousands of borrower-defense claims. The Trump administration stalled them, and borrowers sued. Then in June 2022, the Biden-Harris administration canceled $5.8 billion in student debt for former Corinthian students.

Here's my read: the Debt Collective's real innovation wasn't the strike — it was the research. They found a loaded gun sitting in a statute book for twenty years that nobody had fired, and they built a tool so ordinary people could pull the trigger. That pattern is repeatable. The law is full of provisions written for the powerful that, read carefully, cut the other way. Find them. Build the tool. Bring friends.

A note on the label: organizing debtors is legal. Actually refusing to pay your loans has real consequences — wrecked credit, wage garnishment on federal loans, tax refund offsets. The Corinthian strikers knew what they were risking and did it as a public, collective action with lawyers involved. Don't confuse a coordinated legal strategy with just... not paying your bills and hoping. This book is about power, not about getting your wages garnished alone in your apartment.

Stop Banking With the Enemy

Sometimes the economic weapon isn't a boycott — it's just leaving. Credit unions versus banks is the clearest version:

  • A credit union is a not-for-profit cooperative owned by its members, run by a volunteer board elected by the members. Surplus goes back to members as lower fees, lower loan rates, and higher savings rates.
  • A bank is a for-profit company owned by shareholders. Surplus goes to shareholders. You are the product, not the owner.
  • Your deposits at a federally insured credit union are protected up to $250,000 per share owner by the NCUA (National Credit Union Administration) — the same coverage level the FDIC gives bank depositors, through a different agency.

In 2011, Bank of America announced a $5/month debit card fee — charging you for the privilege of accessing your own money — and the internet revolted. An organizer declared November 5, 2011 "Bank Transfer Day": move your money to a credit union.

The numbers on how many people actually moved are a case study in this book's labeling rule. The Credit Union National Association — the industry's own advocacy group — initially claimed 650,000 new credit union members between late September and November 5. Then on December 6, 2011, CUNA walked it back: the real number was 214,000 new members in October. (The claim of 40,000 joiners on November 5 itself stood.) Present it as what it is: an advocacy group's estimate, revised downward when the quarterly data came in. The direction was real — hundreds of thousands of people moved their money — but the headline number was hype, corrected by the same people who issued it. Honest movements correct themselves.

Own the Job: Worker Cooperatives

If boycotts are about withholding money from bad institutions, cooperatives are about building good ones so you don't need the bad ones at all. A worker cooperative is a business owned and democratically governed by its workers — one worker, one vote. Profits get shared instead of extracted by outside shareholders.

Two examples, because this isn't theory:

Mondragon, Spain. Founded April 14, 1956, by a priest — Father José María Arizmendiarrieta — and former students of his technical college, in a poor Basque town. It grew into a federation of worker cooperatives spanning finance, industry, retail, and research. In 2024 it reported €11.213 billion in revenue and 70,085 employees. Seventy thousand worker-owners. That's not a commune; that's an economy.

Cooperative Home Care Associates, the Bronx. Founded in 1985 with 12 home health aides. Today it's 2,000+ staff — 98% Latina and African-American women — and the largest worker cooperative in the United States. Workers can buy an equal ownership stake. And here's the detail that matters: the co-op model in home care is associated with far lower turnover than the for-profit industry. When workers own the place, they stay. When they stay, the care is better. Ownership isn't just ideology; it's a business advantage.

Here's my read: the cooperative is the most underrated weapon in this whole chapter. Boycotts end. Strikes settle. But a co-op, once it's running, feeds people every single day for decades — and it teaches everyone who works there that the boss isn't a law of nature. You don't have to start with seventy thousand people. Mondragon started with a priest and his students. Cooperative Home Care started with twelve aides. Start with whoever's in the room.

DO THIS: Plan a Boycott Around Achievable Demands

Boycotts fail when they're vague. "Boycott everything bad" is a mood, not a plan. Here's how to build one that can actually win:

1. Pick one winnable demand. Not "end injustice." One thing, specific, measurable: drop the fee, sign the contract, divest the stock, reinstate the worker. If you can't say it in one sentence, it's not a demand yet. Montgomery: desegregate the buses. Delano: sign union contracts. Columbia 1985: divest from apartheid. One sentence each.

2. Pick a target that feels the pressure. Don't boycott the abstract system — boycott the specific company, campus, or office whose money or reputation moves when you move. Huerta's genius was boycotting the grocery chains, not just the growers: she found the pressure point two steps down the supply chain. Ask: who loses money if we do this? Who gets embarrassed? Aim there.

3. Build the support system first. A boycott is a siege, and sieges need supply lines. Montgomery had the carpool network. You've got group chats, rideshare funds, shared spreadsheets, and — don't forget — the mutual aid pod from Chapter 12. People can't sustain a boycott if it costs them their job or their groceries. Build the thing that makes it survivable before you launch. The support system is the boycott; the announcement is just paperwork.

4. Escalate in steps. Start with the ask: a letter, a meeting, a petition. Then the public ask. Then the boycott. Then the secondary boycott (the stores that sell the thing, the sponsors of the thing). Each step gives the target a chance to fold — and each refusal recruits more people to your side, because nothing radicalizes like being ignored politely. Delano's five-year timeline wasn't a failure of escalation; it was the escalation.

5. Name the victory condition in advance. Write it down before you start: "We win when X happens." This protects you from two traps — quitting early because you're tired, and moving the goalposts forever because winning feels strange. When the 26 growers signed on July 29, 1970, the UFW knew it had won that round, because it had defined the round. Name it, win it, say so out loud, then pick the next fight.

Costs, honestly: boycotts cost the boycotters more than the targets, at first. You'll pay more for the alternative grapes, walk further to the alternative store, spend evenings organizing instead of resting. That's the price of leverage, and it's real. Go in with your eyes open and your pod behind you.

Sources and further reading

  • BlackPast.org — "Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56)": the dates, the 381 days, the Browder v. Gayle timeline.
  • Facing History & Ourselves — materials on the Delano grape strike and boycott (citing Matt Garcia, From the Jaws of Victory): the 43% shipment drop, the July 29, 1970 contracts.
  • UFW.org and the Digital Public Library of America — primary-source collections on the farmworker movement.
  • Convergence Magazine interview with Gerald Lenoir — the campus divestment movement's scale, from someone who was there.
  • University of Michigan "Divestment for Humanity" exhibit — the UC and California divestment figures, the Anti-Apartheid Act vote counts.
