Chapter 14 — Lock Your Digital Doors

Your phone is the single most dangerous thing you carry into a fight. Not because of anything you've done on it — because of what it knows. Where you've been, who you talk to, when you talk, what you read, where you sleep. The content of your messages is only part of the story. The rest of it is the part nobody reads the fine print about, and it's the part that does the most damage.

This chapter is digital hygiene, and I mean that literally. Hygiene isn't exciting. You don't win points for it. You do it because the alternative is preventable misery. Nobody romanticizes brushing their teeth, and nobody should romanticize a subpoena. Everything in here is defensive. It's about locking your own doors, not picking anyone else's. If you're looking for the offensive stuff — the hacking, the doxxing, the leaking — it isn't here, and it isn't coming in a later chapter either. This book is nonviolent all the way down, and that includes the keyboard.

What Signal protects — and what it doesn't

Here's what I'd actually tell a friend: get Signal.

Signal is free and open-source, end-to-end encrypted through the Signal Protocol — that's the same encryption protocol WhatsApp later adopted. It's run by a nonprofit. It does not store the contents of your messages. When people in this work say "use an encrypted messenger," they mean this one, and they mean it for good reason.

But here's the thing about encryption: it protects the contents of your messages. It does not protect everything. Understanding the difference is the whole ballgame, so let's be precise.

Metadata: the stuff that gets you

Metadata is everything about a communication except its content. Who called whom. When. For how long. Where each of you was standing. The subject line of the email. The length of the conversation. All the facts about the message, minus what the message said.

The EFF puts it this way: "Even a tiny sample of metadata can provide an intimate lens into a person's life." And here's the kicker — metadata has historically had weaker legal protection in the U.S. than message content. Police can often get your call records far more easily than they can get a wiretap on your actual conversations. The law treats the envelope as less private than the letter, even though the envelope can tell you who's sleeping with whom.

Here's my read: this is the part most people sleep on, because "metadata" sounds boring and technical. It is neither. It's the most dangerous data you generate.

Don't take my word for it. Take it from the people who built the machine that collects it.

In a 2014 debate at Johns Hopkins, former NSA and CIA director Gen. Michael Hayden — a man who ran both agencies — said it plain: "We kill people based on metadata." That's an established fact, on video, from the man himself. Not an activist claim. The director of the NSA, talking about how the United States picks drone targets.

Former NSA General Counsel Stewart Baker said: "Metadata absolutely tells you everything about somebody's life. If you have enough metadata, you don't really need content." Also on the record.

And the courts have noticed. In Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 296 (2018), the Supreme Court held 5–4 that police need a warrant supported by probable cause to get historical cell-site location information. That's an established holding. The case behind it: the FBI had used 127 days of Carpenter's location records — 12,898 individual location points — obtained under a much lower legal standard, to convict him of armed robberies. The Court said no. You want the full picture of where someone has been, every hour of the day, for months? Come back with a warrant.

That's the law as of Carpenter — but note the label here. That's current federal law on that specific type of data. Digital privacy law is jurisdiction-dependent and changes. What protects you in one state may not protect you in another, and the rules keep getting rewritten. Act accordingly.

Back to Signal: this is where Signal stands out. Signal collects almost nothing. When law enforcement comes knocking, the most Signal can hand over is the account creation date and the date of last connection, accurate to the day. That's it. There is no message archive to seize, no contact graph sitting on a server, because Signal didn't keep one. That's not a marketing claim — it's what their published transparency responses show. Signal also has a feature called Sealed Sender, which hides the sender's identity from Signal's own servers. Even the company running the thing can't easily say who wrote to whom.

But — and I want this in capital letters in your head — Signal does not make you invisible. It encrypts the content. It minimizes the metadata. It does not eliminate the phone itself from the equation, and the phone is a tracking device that happens to make calls.

Caveats, because there always are:

  • Signal requires a phone number to register. There are now usernames that can hide your number from people who don't already have it, which is a real improvement. But the number exists in the system. That's a fact about the architecture.
  • Verify safety numbers with close contacts. Signal lets you compare encryption keys with the people you're talking to, to make sure nobody's sitting in the middle. Do this in person with the people who matter. It takes thirty seconds.
  • Disappearing messages are worth turning on. They don't stop anyone from screenshotting while a conversation is happening. What they do is limit what sits on the device if it's seized later. Less stored means less found.

Why SMS is not secure (and what to do about two-factor)

SMS is not secure. Not "a little insecure." Not "secure enough for casual use." It is unencrypted by protocol — the message travels in plaintext through carrier SMS centers, and it can be intercepted in transit. That is an established fact about how SMS works.

The plumbing underneath is worse. SMS and much of the world's phone signaling runs on a system called SS7, a protocol roughly forty years old, built for a time when phone networks trusted each other by default. SS7 has no authentication between networks — an architectural flaw, not a bug — which means attackers can exploit it for location tracking, call and text interception, and stealing one-time login codes. A 2017 U.S. Department of Homeland Security assessment concluded that all U.S. carriers are vulnerable to SS7 and its modern successor Diameter exploits. All of them. That's the government's own security people saying so.

Add SIM-swap attacks — someone convinces your carrier to move your number to their phone — and the fact that carriers retain your message records and metadata, and you get the practical conclusion: do not use SMS for two-factor authentication. Use an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, whatever you can get) or a hardware security key. Texted codes can be intercepted, redirected, and stolen in ways app-generated codes can't. This is one of the cheapest, highest-impact things you can do, and you can do it tonight.

Protest phone hygiene, ranked

People ask me what to do with their phone at a protest. Here's the honest ranking, strongest first. No single option is perfect; each one is a trade-off. Pick with your eyes open.

1. Don't bring the phone. This is the EFF's own recommendation, and it's the strongest move by a mile. You can't be tracked by a thing that isn't there, and a thing that isn't there can't be seized. I know this is annoying. I know you want the camera and the map and the group chat. The trade-off is real. But the honest ranking starts here: the phone you leave at home creates no new risk from that device. The people who do this work seriously leave the primary phone home and, if they need one, some bring a cheap minimal phone with nothing on it — that's an option organizers discuss, not a standard I'm certifying.

2. Powered off. Stronger than airplane mode for preventing remote tracking. Off is off. But — flag — a powered-off phone still contains everything stored on it if it's seized. The contents are still there; the power state just stops it from talking to towers in real time.

3. A Faraday bag. It blocks all radio-frequency signals — cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, all of it. The phone goes dark to the network without having to be powered down. But here's the caveat the briefs always bury in the footnotes: test the bag before you rely on it. Call the phone while it's in the bag. If it rings, the bag is a wallet, not a shield. Cheap ones fail. Test them.

4. Airplane mode. This disables the cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth radios, which mitigates real-time location tracking. The EFF's own technologist, Bill Budington, called it "pretty good" — and I want you to hear the honesty in that phrase. Pretty good. Not perfect. Because here's the second half of the fact: airplane mode does not protect data already on the phone against forensic extraction if the phone is seized. It stops the phone from phoning home. It doesn't stop the contents from being read off the device by someone holding it.

So the ranking is: absent beats off beats bag beats airplane mode. And every option below "absent" still leaves your stored data exposed if someone physically takes the phone.

Passcode versus biometrics: the uncomfortable truth

Here's the EFF's 2020 guidance, and it's worth quoting exactly: "In the U.S., law currently provides stronger protection against police forcing you to enter a passcode than forcing you to biometrically unlock your device." So: at protests, disable Touch ID and Face ID and use a long passcode — the EFF suggests 8–12 random characters.

Now the label matters, because the law here is genuinely unsettled. This is a general principle, not settled law, and it's jurisdiction-dependent and evolving:

  • A memorized passcode is treated by many courts as testimonial — it's something in your head, and compelling you to reveal it runs into the Fifth Amendment's privilege against self-incrimination.
  • Biometrics — your face, your fingerprint — are treated by some courts as non-testimonial, like being compelled to give a blood sample. A recent Ninth Circuit decision held that compelled biometric unlock does not violate the privilege against self-incrimination.
  • The legal distinction is evolving and jurisdiction-dependent. What holds in one federal circuit may not hold in another, and this area of law is actively being litigated.

Here's my read: the direction of travel is not in your favor. Courts have a habit of catching up with technology by shrinking your protections, not expanding them. So treat the EFF's advice as the floor, not the ceiling — disable biometrics when it matters, use the long passcode — but don't build your plan on the assumption that any court will save you. The best protection is not having the data on the device in the first place.

The group chat is the weakest link

One more thing, because this is where most real-world exposure actually happens: the group chat.

Here's my read, and it's pure analysis, no citation needed because it's logic: your personal phone can be a fortress and it won't matter if the planning happens in a group chat where one person has cloud backups turned on, another screenshots everything "just in case," and a third added their cousin who nobody's met. The security of a group conversation is set by its least careful member. Always. There is no app that fixes that.

So the hygiene has to be social, not just technical. Agree on the rules out loud: what's Signal-only, what never goes in writing at all, who gets added to what. The conversations that matter most — the sensitive ones — happen face to face, with phones in another room. That sounds paranoid until you remember that a phone in the room can be a microphone. Treat it like one. It's not paranoia. It's just physics plus business models.

And keep the circles small. Not because you don't trust people — because every additional person is another phone, another backup setting, another set of habits you don't control. The inner circle plans in person. The outer circle gets the public announcements. That's not hierarchy; that's hygiene.

The organizer's digital-hygiene checklist: do this week

Enough theory. Here's the practical list. You can do all of this without spending a dollar and without being a technical person.

1. Move your real conversations to Signal. Download it, get your core people on it, turn on disappearing messages. Keep the safety-number verification for the people who matter most. This is the single highest-value move on the list.

2. Kill SMS two-factor everywhere. Go through your accounts — email first, then banking, then social media — and switch every two-factor method from texted codes to an authenticator app. If you can get a hardware security key for your most important accounts, even better. Tonight if possible. This week at the latest.

3. Set a long passcode. Eight to twelve random characters, per the EFF. Not your birthday. Not the pattern your ex could guess. Random. Write it on paper kept somewhere safe until it's in your muscle memory.

4. Disable biometrics before any action. Make it a habit, the way you check your pockets for your keys. Face ID off, fingerprint off, long passcode on, before you leave for anything that might get interesting.

5. Decide your phone policy for actions in advance. Don't improvise in the parking lot. Decide now: for which situations does the phone stay home? Who's the designated person who keeps one for emergencies? What's the backup plan if nobody has one? Write it down. Tell people. A plan you made calmly beats a plan you made in a hurry, every time.

6. Minimize what the phone knows. Location history: off or regularly deleted. Old messages with sensitive content: delete them, or let disappearing messages do it for you. App permissions: audit them — half your apps are collecting location data they have no business holding. Every byte the phone holds is a byte someone else can demand.

7. Back up what's important, somewhere you control. Photos, contacts, documents — backed up to an encrypted drive you physically hold, or a service you trust, before you walk into anything. Because the flip side of "don't carry sensitive data" is "don't lose the stuff you actually need."

8. Have the conversation. Digital hygiene is a team sport. You can have perfect habits and still get exposed by a group chat where one person screenshots everything and stores it in iCloud. Talk to your people. Agree on the norms. The weakest phone in the group chat sets the security of the whole chat.

And the part nobody likes to hear: none of this makes you invincible. Every one of these measures raises the cost of surveilling you. That's the goal — not invincibility, but cost. The machine has unlimited money and patience for one person. It does not have unlimited money and patience for ten thousand people who all made themselves expensive to watch. Your locked door doesn't stop a determined nation-state. It stops the casual, automated, dragnet kind of watching, which is the kind that does most of the damage to movements. Lock your doors. Make them work for it. Move on to the next thing.

Chapter 15 — Build the Replacement

Every movement that only protests eventually runs out of breath. You can march until your feet bleed, and if there's nowhere to go after the march, the machine just waits you out. It has patience. It has pensions. It can outlast your anger.

The movements that last build something. They build the replacement — institutions that feed people, house people, heal people, without asking the machine's permission. Not as a charity project. As a base of operations. As proof that the world you're fighting for already works, in miniature, right now.

This is the least glamorous chapter in the book and the most important one. Nobody makes a movie about the land trust board meeting. But the land trust is still there after the cameras leave, and that's the whole point.

The idea

A parallel institution is a thing that does what the system is supposed to do — housing, healthcare, food, money — but runs on different rules. The system's rules are: extract, concentrate, exclude. The parallel institution's rules are: meet the need, share the power, include everybody.

Here's my read on why this works as resistance, not just charity: it changes the leverage. A community that can house itself is harder to evict into compliance. A community that can feed itself is harder to starve into compliance. A community that can heal itself is harder to scare into compliance. Every need you meet yourselves is a lever the machine can't pull. That's not a metaphor — that's mechanics.

And there's a second reason, quieter but just as real: it teaches the people building it that they're capable. Nothing radicalizes like competence. The moment a neighborhood realizes it can run its own clinic, the story that "we need them" starts to rot. You can't unlearn that.

Land: the Dudley Street story

Housing is the sharpest lever in America, because housing is where the money lives and where displacement happens. A community land trust takes the land out of the speculation game. The model: a nonprofit owns the land; residents own the homes on it, typically through long-term ground leases. The land stays in community hands permanently. Prices can't spiral, because the land beneath the house isn't for sale to the highest bidder.

The proof-of-concept is in Roxbury, Boston. The Dudley Street Neighborhood Initiative — DSNI — was founded in 1984 by residents and the Riley Foundation, with a simple slogan: "development without displacement." The neighborhood had been hollowed out — arson, dumping, absentee landlords, the city treating it like a write-off.

What DSNI did next had never been done. It became the first — and still the only — community-run organization in the United States granted eminent domain authority, by the Boston Redevelopment Authority. Read that again. The power to take land for public purpose — the power governments use to clear neighborhoods for highways and stadiums — was handed to the neighborhood itself. DSNI used it to assemble the roughly 64-acre Dudley Triangle into a community land trust: affordable housing, community gardens, green space, all of it under community control, permanently.

And the governance: DSNI is run by an elected 35-member board representing the neighborhood's four major ethnic groups. Not a charity board of downtown donors. The people who live there, electing the people who decide.

Those are established facts — Massachusetts Historical Society, the trust's own records, the works. And here's what they mean, my read: the most radical thing DSNI did wasn't taking the land. It was proving that a poor neighborhood could be trusted with the powers of a government and use them better than the government had. The city had decades to fix Dudley Street and produced rubble. The residents got the authority and produced homes. Remember that the next time someone tells you communities can't govern themselves.

Health: the clinics they tried to kill

If you want to understand what parallel institutions cost — and what they prove — look at the free clinics.

The Black Panther Party's People's Free Medical Clinics, 1969 to 1975: thirteen clinics across the country. (Flag, because honesty matters here: some sources say fourteen. I'm going with thirteen, from BlackPast.org, and noting the disagreement.) They did checkups, vaccinations, basic screening — the unglamorous work of keeping poor people alive.

And then they did something that changed national policy. Starting in 1971, the clinics ran a national sickle cell anemia screening and education program — at a time when the medical establishment largely neglected the disease. Sickle cell overwhelmingly affects Black Americans. The establishment's neglect wasn't an oversight; it was a pattern. The Panthers' program is credited with pressuring Congress to pass the National Sickle Cell Anemia Control Act of 1972. A free clinic in a church basement, run by people the FBI called the greatest threat to internal security, moved the United States Congress. Sit with that.

The Winston-Salem clinic ran a free ambulance service. The clinics were met with health-inspector harassment and police raids — the standard welcome. Of all thirteen, only one survives: Seattle's, reopened in 1978 as the Carolyn Downs Family Medical Center, still operating.

The Panthers weren't the only ones. On July 14, 1970, the Young Lords — a Puerto Rican activist group modeled on the Panthers — occupied Lincoln Hospital in the South Bronx for twelve hours. They raised the Puerto Rican flag over it and renamed it "The People's Hospital" — "Bienvenidos al hospital del pueblo." Seven demands: a new hospital building, higher wages for workers, day care, door-to-door testing for lead poisoning, tuberculosis, and anemia.

Two occupiers were arrested; the charges were dismissed. (Flag: sources disagree on how many people took part — around 150 by one count, 50 by another. The twelve-hour duration is consistent.) The action is credited with helping establish one of the first Patient's Bill of Rights in the country. And it was part of a broader health offensive: the "Garbage Offensive" for sanitation services, door-to-door lead-poisoning testing in neighborhoods the city had written off, the seizure of a city TB X-ray truck to take screening to the people instead of waiting for the people to come to the system.

Those are established facts — HISTORY.com, the Zinn Education Project, the movement's own records. Here's my read: notice the pattern. The Panthers and the Young Lords didn't just demand better healthcare. They provided it, badly under-resourced, while demanding it. The providing was the argument. You can't tell people "trust us, we could run this better" — but you can show them a clinic, a screening program, an ambulance that comes when you call. Parallel institutions don't argue that the replacement works. They demonstrate it.

The tradition didn't die with the seventies. The National Association of Free & Charitable Clinics (NAFC), founded in 2001, now supports more than 1,400 clinics whose 200,000+ volunteers and staff provide care to more than 2 million patients a year. That's not a protest. That's a healthcare system, running parallel to the official one, treating millions of people the official one priced out. Quietly. Every day.

What a parallel institution needs to survive

This is the practical part, and I'm going to be blunt, because romanticism kills more good projects than opposition does. Starting the thing is the easy part. Keeping it alive is the work. Here's what the ones that survived had in common:

1. A real need, not a good idea. The breakfast program worked because children were hungry. The clinics worked because people were sick and couldn't pay. DSNI worked because people were being displaced. Every surviving parallel institution on record started from a need so concrete you could point at it. "Wouldn't it be cool if we had a..." is not a need. "People on this block can't get X and are suffering without it" is a need. Start there or don't start.

2. A real base. Not followers — a base. People who show up, who are accountable to each other, who can't just log off. The land trust had a neighborhood. The clinics had chapters. The mutual aid networks that lasted had block captains and regulars. A mailing list is not a base. A base is people who will carry boxes in the rain.

3. A legal form. This is the boring one, and it's non-negotiable. A nonprofit, a cooperative, a trust — something that exists on paper, holds the assets, and can't be dissolved by one person's bad week. DSNI's eminent domain authority meant nothing without the organizational form to wield it. The clinics that survived harassment were the ones with enough legal standing to fight back. Get the paperwork. Pay the filing fees. It's the least revolutionary-sounding advice in this book and one of the most important.

4. Money that can't be pulled. Here's the trap: if your funding comes from one foundation, one donor, or one grant, your institution belongs to them, not to the community. The moment you do something they don't like, the money walks. Diversify from day one — small donations from the base, earned revenue if the model allows it, multiple funders, reserves. The goal is that no single person or institution can kill you by closing a checkbook. Financial independence is political independence. That's not a slogan; it's accounting.

5. The ability to survive harassment. This is the one nobody wants to plan for, so plan for it now. The Panther clinics faced health-inspector harassment and police raids. The breakfast program was a named COINTELPRO target — the FBI's own memos say so. If your institution matters, it will attract attention from people who'd rather it didn't exist. That means: know your legal rights (Part III of this book), keep your paperwork clean, document everything, have a lawyer's number before you need it, and build the kind of community support that makes shutting you down politically expensive. An institution the whole neighborhood depends on is harder to raid than a storefront nobody visits. Popularity is armor.

And one more, because it underlies all five: start small enough to survive being bad at it. The first Panther breakfast served 11 kids. Eleven. DSNI started as meetings in living rooms. The NAFC's 1,400 clinics started as one. You don't need the full vision on day one. You need eleven kids fed, one block organized, one need met — and then you do it again next week. The boring repetition is the institution. Everything else is decoration.

Why the machine fears the replacement most

Here's my read, and I'll label it as mine because it's analysis, not a sourced claim: of everything in this book — the boycotts, the strikes, the debt organizing, the digital hygiene — the parallel institution is the one the machine genuinely can't digest. It can wait out a protest. It can absorb a boycott's losses and write them off. It can even survive losing a court case. What it can't do is compete with a working alternative.

A boycott says "stop buying this." A parallel institution says "you don't need them at all." The first is pressure. The second is obsolescence. Pressure can be negotiated with; obsolescence can't. That's why the breakfast program got a COINTELPRO memo and a police raid, while a hundred angry marches got traffic cones. Marches ask the machine to change. The breakfast program proved the machine was unnecessary. One of those is a request. The other is a threat.

And notice: building the replacement is the one tactic in this book that works even if you never win a single confrontation. Every meal served is a win that doesn't require anyone's permission. Every patient treated, every family kept in their home, every dollar moved from a bank to a credit union — these are victories that don't depend on the other side conceding anything. You don't need them to lose. You just need your people to eat. That makes it the most resilient strategy in the book, because it can't be defeated by any single defeat. A boycott can break. A court case can be lost. A network of 1,400 clinics that treated two million patients last year is a fact on the ground, and facts on the ground are very hard to unmake.

Start with the need in front of you. Build the thing that meets it. Make it boring, make it regular, make it last. That's the whole strategy, and it's enough.

Closing: The Boring Revolution

Here we are. End of the book.

If you've read straight through, you now know how the machine works — the wealth, the coordination, the incentives that keep it all turning whether anyone's conspiring or not. You've met people like you who beat pieces of it: the boycotters, the strikers, the debtors who organized and got billions canceled. You've got the legal shield — what the law actually says, where it protects you, where it doesn't, and how to stay on the right side of the line while standing as close to it as you dare. And in this last part, you got the tools: feed people, hit the wallets, lock your digital doors, build the replacement.

Now I'm going to tell you the thesis of this whole book, the thing I'd tattoo on the cover if the publisher would let me:

The most dangerous book you can write about fighting back is the boring one.

Not the one with the secret plan. Not the one with the dramatic confrontation. The boring one. The one that says: organize. Starve them economically. Build the replacement. Repeat until it works.

Nobody fantasizes about the boring revolution. There's no movie scene where the hero files nonprofit paperwork. Nobody gets goosebumps at "diversify your funding streams so no single donor can kill you." The breakfast program's most radical act wasn't a speech — it was feeding a kid eggs on a Tuesday, and then doing it again Wednesday, for years. The land trust's most radical act was a board meeting. The clinic's most radical act was a vaccination. The boycott's most radical act was walking to work in the rain for 381 days.

Here's my read, and I'll label it because it's mine: the machine wants you to think revolution is an event. An event has a date. A date can be surrounded. An event ends, and then everyone goes home, and the machine is still there on Monday morning, because the machine never went home. The machine is a routine. The only thing that beats a routine is a better routine, run longer, by more people.

So the work is unglamorous. It's meetings. It's showing up when it's raining. It's the tenth phone-banking shift, the hundredth meal served, the thousandth door knocked. It's learning the boring skills — bookkeeping, filing deadlines, running a meeting where everyone gets heard and it still ends on time. It's locking your digital doors when nothing's happening, so the habit's there when something is. It's building the clinic before you need the clinic to be a fortress.

And it's slow. The Montgomery boycott took 381 days. The grape boycott took five years. The Dudley Street trust took decades to become what it is. Anyone who promises you a fast revolution is selling you something — probably a book, possibly a disaster. The real ones took years, and the people who won them were ordinary people who refused to stop doing the boring thing.

I wrote in the foreword, and I'll say it again here because it's the whole book in one line: the machine doesn't care what it hits. I decided to care.

The machine will process you the same way it processes everyone — as an input, a data point, a pair of hands, a wallet. It doesn't hate you. Hate would be personal. It's worse than hate: it's indifference with a spreadsheet. The only answer to a machine that doesn't care is people who do. Not performatively. Not for the cameras. Actually. The woman who makes sure the community fridge is stocked. The neighbor who shows up with the truck. The organizer who does the paperwork. The person who locks their digital door and teaches everyone else to lock theirs.

That's the boring revolution. No capes. No slogans that rhyme. Just people who decided to care, doing the unglamorous work, refusing to stop.

So close the book. Put it down. And go do the boring thing — today, not someday. Find the eleven kids. Feed them. Then do it again tomorrow.

The machine is patient. Be more patient.
